app_info.name: Untitled Goose Game
app_info.detailed_description:
It's a lovely morning in the village and you are a horrible goose.

Untitled Goose Game is a slapstick-stealth-sandbox, where you are a goose let loose on an unsuspecting village. Make your way around town, from peoples' back gardens to the high street shops to the village green, setting up pranks, stealing hats, honking a lot, and generally ruining everyone’s day.

Featuring:

  • A horrible goose (that's you)
  • A town full of people just trying to get on with their day (you hate them)
  • A dedicated honk button (!!!)

AND ALSO

Oh dear! Two horrible geese!

You can now enjoy Untitled Goose Game with a friend, in a new two-player cooperative mode. Play through the whole game as two horrible geese, honking twice as much, teaming up to plan pranks, and generally ruining everyone's day, together.

  • A free update for all owners of Untitled Goose Game
  • Play through the entire game with two players
  • New goose, new honk, still horrible

reviews.review:

Untitled Goose Game is a charming, offbeat, and surprisingly clever stealth-puzzle experience where you play as a single, chaotic goose let loose in a quaint English village. Developed by House House, the game flips traditional game structure on its head by giving players no heroic journey, no tragic backstory, and no need to save the world—just a to-do list and a goose’s burning desire to make life inconvenient for everyone. This simplicity is what makes the game instantly appealing. With its minimalist aesthetic, comedic tone, and intuitive mechanics, Untitled Goose Game crafts a unique identity that’s both absurdly funny and sneakily brilliant.

From the moment you waddle out of the bushes and honk your first honk, the game sets the tone perfectly. You’re not just a bird—you’re a troublemaker with a mission. The core gameplay loop revolves around completing a list of mischievous tasks that range from mildly annoying to full-blown sabotage. These include stealing items from picnic baskets, tricking villagers into misplacing their glasses, and locking shopkeepers out of their own stores. While the objectives seem simple, solving them often requires creative thinking, timing, and manipulating the AI of unsuspecting townsfolk. This turns the game into a blend of sandbox experimentation and light stealth, not unlike a feathered version of Hitman—if Agent 47’s goals were centered on embarrassing people rather than eliminating them.

Visually, the game is minimalist but beautifully stylized. The soft, painterly art direction gives the village a storybook quality that’s pleasant to explore but not too distracting. The characters have a deliberately stiff, almost puppet-like movement style that makes them perfect comedic foils for your schemes. Audio is used sparingly but effectively. The standout is the reactive classical piano score that rises and falls based on your actions—adding a layer of whimsy and slapstick charm to even the smallest interactions. There’s no dialogue, but the game doesn’t need it. Every moment is readable, expressive, and intuitive thanks to great animation and clever sound design.

The village itself is divided into interconnected zones, each with its own unique challenges and routines. As you progress, the goose's antics cause escalating levels of disruption, opening new areas and harder tasks. Despite its short length—most players can complete the main objectives in a few hours—the game packs a lot of variety into a small space. After the credits roll, an expanded to-do list becomes available, offering more challenging versions of previous tasks and encouraging replayability. There’s even a speedrun mode and a two-player co-op option added post-launch, which turns the chaos up exponentially and provides hilarious opportunities for synchronized honking and double-teaming mischief.

What elevates Untitled Goose Game from a novelty to something truly memorable is how it invites players to think like a goose. It’s not just about ticking off tasks; it’s about role-playing as a disruptive force in an orderly world. There's a subtle layer of social commentary underneath the chaos—how one unpredictable element can unravel routine and order, how power can be expressed through pettiness, and how games don’t need to rely on violence or grand stakes to be compelling. It’s a sandbox where the goal isn’t dominance, but mischief, and that’s a rare and refreshing take.

If there’s a criticism to be made, it’s that the novelty wears a bit thin during repeat playthroughs. The AI can be inconsistent, sometimes leading to solutions that feel more like accidents than clever strategies. Also, the small size of the world means that once you've figured out the puzzles, there's little incentive to return unless you’re aiming for perfection or co-op chaos. Still, the game is self-aware about its scale and never overstays its welcome. It’s short, but densely packed with personality.

Ultimately, Untitled Goose Game is a delightful subversion of gaming norms. It shows how minimalism in design, combined with a singularly odd concept, can create something that resonates widely. Its success lies not just in its humor, but in how well-crafted every element is, from the responsive controls to the dynamic music and environmental storytelling. It’s a game that makes you laugh not through scripted jokes, but through the sheer joy of being a goose doing awful goose things. Whether you play it once or return for more honking havoc, it’s an experience that’s hard to forget and easy to recommend.

Rating: 9/10

[b]PROS:[/b]
+ hilarious gameplay
+ fantastic visual style
+ plenty of stuff to do

[b]CONS:[/b]

[b]Comment:[/b]
What a game! Crazy fun concept of waddling around, causing mischief and not giving a honk about what the humans think. And sure, some of them will shoo you away or take the thing you just stole. But that is the maximum they can do. They cannot hurt you. They will not stop the chaos honk train rolling through their village, only delay it.

Gameplay is simple - you can honk at, run from and grab what you want with the stuff/people you find. Or you can move onto the to-do list(s) which contain specific tasks. There are four main areas that unlock as you progress in the to-do lists. And you can unlock shortcuts (gates) to the previous areas in this way too. Simple premise but the execution takes a bit of practice.

I played this with my son and we had a blast (for the most part). We laughed many times and improved our teamwork as we figured out the mechanics. Which is why I recommend going in blind at least for the first playthrough. Discovering is part of the charm this game has. The game is VERY kid friendly, you have as many attempts as you like. Though the action heats up towards the end where you have to outrun and outmaneuver the citizens.

Having finished both solo and co-op I can say that I found it easier to go solo. But it is FAR more fun to play with someone else! Playing co-op in the later areas requires a level of coordination because you can only get a certain distance from your fellow goose. This can become super restricting in some places, especially the pub one.

So whether you are a solo player or want to give this a go with someone else - this game is plenty of fun! It scratches that itch of being goofy enough to enjoy casually but also making room for more skill (or cooperation) based play. Recommended!

Untitled Goose Game is a short, physics-based stealth-puzzle game where you play as a goose causing problems across a small village. Its focus is simple: complete chaotic objectives through mischief and manipulation.

Movement feels clean and responsive. The physics are grounded enough to make every interaction feel real. Dragging, stealing, and dropping items all behave as expected, which helps sell the illusion that you're not just playing a goose, but embodying one.

I played the way the game clearly wants you to. In one task, I untied a kid’s shoes, watched him fall into a puddle, stole his glasses, swapped them with the wrong pair, took his toy, put it up for sale, and chased him into a phone booth. The game handled every part of that sequence smoothly. It supports chaos without falling apart.

Objectives encourage creative thinking. Most puzzles reward playful experimentation rather than logic. A few hidden tasks added replay value, though some goals could have used clearer direction. A simple hint system would’ve helped in a couple spots.

There’s no upgrade system or extended progression, but the length feels right. It ends before it wears thin.

Visually, it’s clean and stylized. Sound design is excellent. The music rises and falls based on your actions, and every honk, flap, and step feels sharp. There's no dialogue, but each scene is full of personality.

Untitled Goose Game delivers exactly what it promises. It’s a compact, polished experience built around harmless disruption. If that speaks to you, it’s worth your time.

Final Rating: 8/10

I played it for Play or Pay 3rd Cycle of 2025 and it was picked for me by Aldrow.

Untitled Goose Game is just pure, honking chaos—and I mean that in the best way possible. From the moment I waddled into the unsuspecting village as a grumpy little goose, I knew I was in for something special. There’s no deep lore or emotional journey here—just a goose with a to-do list and a deep-rooted need to mess with everyone’s day. And it’s hilarious.

The art style is so simple yet so charming. The soft colors and storybook aesthetic make the village feel cozy and peaceful… which is the perfect backdrop for the chaos you’re about to unleash. Whether you’re stealing someone’s glasses, locking a kid in a phone booth, or waddling around honking like a maniac, every moment feels like you’re in on a very silly joke.

Gameplay-wise, it’s easy to pick up and really satisfying once you get into the groove of solving each mischievous puzzle. The stealth element is light but fun—you’ll be hiding behind bushes one moment and dashing off with someone’s belongings the next. I played it solo and had a blast, but I’m really looking forward to trying it out in co-op with my husband someday. Two geese? Twice the trouble. Unlimited chaos.

As an achievement hunter, I found most of the achievements to be smooth sailing and really enjoyable. That said, the timed challenges did push my patience a little. There were definitely a few moments where I had to put the controller down before I snapped—but finally pulling them off felt so good. It struck a nice balance between “fun challenge” and “controller yeeting frustration,” which honestly, I respect.

Overall, Untitled Goose Game is one of those rare games that doesn’t overstay its welcome. It’s not too long, not too short, and filled with personality from start to finish. It’s the kind of game you’ll smile about long after finishing it. Highly recommend it if you're looking for something unique, lighthearted, and just a little bit unhinged.

Welcome everyone to my review of Untitled Goose Game!

📜 ~ Enjoy reading!

Untitled Goose Game is a game that allows you to immerse yourself in a world where the main character is a nimble, mischievous goose.

🕹️ Controls.
The controls in the game are quite simple, but unusual.
• To move slowly, you need to select the direction with the mouse, hovering over any part of the screen, then press and hold the LMB once.
• To run, you need to press the LMB twice and hold.
! ~ It is important to remember that it is not very convenient to fit into a turn at full speed, so you can release the mouse button, turn and run again. This will allow you to change the direction of movement without skidding and turn in time.
• You cannot walk at full height everywhere and not all lying objects can be collected without bending down, so you will need the Ctrl key to bend down.
• To grab an object or interact with something, you need to press the RMB and to release it, respectively.
+ You can distract people or celebrate completing a level using the SPACEBAR on the keyboard. When you press it, our main character will cackle.
+ In addition to this, you can flap your wings with the X button.
The last two mechanics (+) give a small but pleasant bonus to immersion!

🎨 Graphics.
The graphics are unique. There is a feeling that the whole game is a large, animated drawing, and this is good in its own way.
The emotions and character of additional characters are expressed not through faces or facial expressions, but through their behavior in various situations and habits.
Even without detailed faces, you understand and imagine them yourself, based on your experience! It's interesting.
You can interact with almost all objects: take something from a shelf, push a ball, drop a bucket or get a carrot from the ground. The next item, called..., is built on the basis of these interactions.

🎮 Gameplay.
After a short tutorial at the beginning of the game, you immediately get access to the to-do list, although in most cases there are more pranks than to-dos! It contains different items, as you complete them, new locations with new tasks will open.
I divided them into two types: collectible - collect items from one/several locations in one place and endurance tasks - interact with any item at the right time to get the desired result.

⚔️ Cooperative game mode.
I completed the game and all the additional tasks myself, but the fact that there is always the opportunity to call a second goose for help makes replays more interesting and you can complete the tasks much faster.
📑 Result: I liked the game, it gives a unique experience and perfectly immerses you in a simple, short, but interesting world!

I definitely recommend it!
9🔔/10🔔

The Untitled Goose Game is not just a game; it's a meticulously researched documentary on the life of an insane criminal mastermind trapped in a foul body. Everything I suspected about gooses--Their mastery of the performance arts, their ability to set a perfectly romantic picnic (by stealing ONLY what's necessary), their baffling capacity for personal space and property--was honked and delivered with 100% accuracy! 

This goose is now my spirit animal, my style icon, and possibly my sibling..

I hate geese because I got attacked by one as a child, but I love games where I get play the monster so I had a lot of fun with Untitled Goose Game.  

It's basically a puzzle game with stealth elements.  Each section of the town has a checklist that the goose has to complete before unlocking the next segment.  There are also several optional tasks as well, and it can be fun trying to figure out all of these.  For those who want a challenge, there are timed checklists that unlock after all of the segments are completed.  

The art style is simple but effective and the animations are expressive.  This game is very British so of course the goose gets to wreak havoc at a pub.  

Most of the activities are easy to perform but there are a couple of fiddly ones.  For example, I got stuck trying to remove a bar stool for awhile but after many attempts I got it to work.  Overall, there is a fair amount of trial and error involved but it's fun to try a variety of different things and watch the citizens freak out and try to hunt me down in various ways.   

The game isn't too long but it offers enough challenge to be satisfying so I recommend it.

Overall: 6.5/10

TLDR: There's definitely a certain joy in being a complete butthole and boy does Untitled Goose Game allow you to fulfill that fantasy. The amount of truly malevolent mischief you can get up to is truly glorious. You can just tell that the creators just loved the idea and spent every second cramming little jokes, with incredible attention to detail in terms of animations and props around the game world. I was frequently impressed by the ideas the developers had to cause some major inconveniences in the town, coined as "tasks" in the to-do list, though I did find myself wishing for more hints or guidance on what I was meant to do. Add on some clunky controls, and I find myself a bit bored at times while I just started to (slowly and painfully with said clunky controls) try random shenanigans and hope they were the "right" thing to do. Luckily, this type of chaotic/open/unstructured gameplay lends to a pretty good multiplayer experience, especially for couch co-op.

Visuals/Style: 7/10

The low-poly style of untitled goose game is obviously not very complex, or probably that create, but it works for this style of game and anything too complicated would have been unnecessary. The low detail could make it difficult to differentiate where objects start and end, but I find the game was pretty good at putting very contrasting colours next to each other so that silhouettes remained clear. The designs of the environment were cute and full of interactable objects you didn't necessarily *need* for your missions, but added to the immersion. The animations were particularly well done, and although all the characters have very simple designs, their emotions (particularly the sweet sweet periods where their mild frustration and annoyance turned into full blown anger) were very clear and made the thrill of mischief all the more fun. That being said, most of the actual settings and character designs are pretty simple and forgettable. While the personalities of the characters made them interesting despite of this, I wouldn't have minded some more interesting designs? I believe that the game benefits from being a more down to earth story, so I understand the designs can't break the immersion of this quaint little town and be *too* zany, but I wish I could actually look back and remember what the artist or newspaper guy looked like.

Gameplay: 4/10

Obligatory I played this on keyboard and mouse (sorry), but I found the movement to be really really clunky. The goose kind of waddles, which makes them awkward to move. While this is understandable for ⋆˙⟡ immersion ✧˖°. , it in the end made for some annoying chase sequences where I couldn't help but feel I would have been fine if I felt like I could actually turn around quicker. Additionally, the grab function never seemed to pick up the object you want if there's a bunch really close together, it felt imprecise, which detracted from the joy of stealing people's things and causing strife. I really don't want to sound like I'm being nitpicky on purpose, and I'm not against games being difficult, but it didn't really feel like this game was challenging my technical ability as much as it ended up being just a bit frustrating at times.

Story: 6/10

Since this game doesn't really have a story other than "you are a goose here to make people in this village hate you", I am opting to put the creative aspects of the puzzles under here to fill it out. Arguably, a story unfolds as you do each task...but yeah I also just didn't want to leave this section empty. I've split the points for the puzzles between story and gameplay.

The actual puzzles themselves on how to do the missions were quite creative or just plain fun. I particularly enjoyed [spoiler]Trapping the boy in the garage, which I didn't even realize was an extra secret task at the time. But seeing the steam achievement when I did it made me burst out loud laughing[/spoiler]. There's [spoiler]5[/spoiler] distinct areas in the game, and I liked that some of the tasks were very specific to the personalities of the people in that setting, or the layout of the setting itself. [spoiler] Rake in the lake, stealing the dart thrower's chair, and making the boy get chastised for stealing were some of my favourites [/spoiler]. The best moments are when you get an evil terrible idea when you see something and go "oh, what if I did this....." or "oh, what if the way to do this is..." and seeing your idea come to fruition.

I do think the last area/level was the most anti-climactic, as it didn't really involve a lot of cleverness so to speak? [spoiler] It's essentially a runback through all of the areas you were in before, carrying a bell. But other than having to create some relatively easy to do distractions, it's almost a straight shot back to your nest [/spoiler]. I would have enjoyed more props or actions to do other than [spoiler]simply having to distract everyone [/spoiler].

[spoiler]I do love the goose's little collection of bells at the end though[/spoiler]

Music/Sound: 9/10

I really didn't expect the music and sound design to be anything other than serviceable. And indeed, it didn't really need to be anything other than that. However, unexpectedly, it ended up being so perfect and *whimsical*. It's the perfect mood, I could hear any of the music play and instantly know it comes from Untitled Goose Game.  Like, if the goose had a soundtrack playing through its mind while it got up to its dastardly deeds, I'd imagine it would sound like this! A bit air-headed but still just a bit malicious. I like that it's a bit cacophony-esque, and is a bit dissonant but still very pleasant sounding. It's very jazzy. I also like that it knows to be silent, indeed the game is silent for large portions of time, minus the padding of your feet and the sound of you causing ruin.

But the game is punctuated by dramatic chords, arpeggios, and small measures that really punctuate when you are doing a task and moving something around that will cause trouble. And the music gets higher, more frantic, faster, the moment the effect of your deeds are being found which is a really clever touch. It makes the whole experience feel almost cinematic, like you're on a charming cute heist with your little goose. I like that there's specific passages that get played when you're being chased too that have a frantic, but still whimsical feel. It's like nothing really feels too serious, the goose is just having fun!

I like how a lot of the sound effects are purposely annoying too when they're meant to annoy the characters around you, like the radio, bell, harmonica. You can almost feel bad for the people you're pissing off. Almost.

Multiplayer: 8/10

I didn't play very much of the multiplayer, and using Steam's remote play probably diminished the enjoyment due to connection issues. However, because it's a game where you can kind of mess around and cause chaos, it was fairly fun. Being able to honk in the face of your friend for 5min is certainly a big draw. Plus, when playing with someone else, I felt like I was a bit more inclined to just try random stuff, since that isn't as much fun to do alone. By doing that, we were able to just run into secret hidden tasks, and it was always a lot of fun to discover one from a crazy one-off idea. The game isn't necessarily super balanced for 2 players so it definitely makes some tasks easier, but since you're really just supposed to be messing around that's okay. If you happen to have a friend over and just feel like playing something lowkey and non-competitive, this is a great pick.

I really enjoyed most of my time with Untitled Goose Game - the silly vibes, the delightful execution, the overall charming aesthetic and the amount of little details scattered all over the game work together to make an enthralling and wonderfully silly experience - changing your honk by honking while picking up different items, being an absolute menace to small children, stealthing into a pub, posing as a statue... the game has a lot of these little moments, where you get to be either an absolute menace, or have a wonderful opportunity to interact with the enviromnent to have something silly happen - like the walkie talkies, or the flowers in the back garden.

That being said, there are some problems that this game has. The controls are... difficult. While i know that this isn't supposed to be a high precision game, the fact that you move like a tank can make careful mobility or speed difficult - further compounded by the fact that there are speedrun achievements which, while somewhat generous with their timing, are still strict enough to cause failiure if you get stuck, or pushed around too long - meaning that the imprecision and clunkiness ends up being a considerable source of frustration. The controls cannot be re-bound either, meaning you have to deal with the unusual layout all the way through, which is generally only a problem when going for the aformentioned speedrun achievements.

Overall though, i had a lot of fun with Untitled Goose Game - only restricted or limited by the fact that i had to try to play a generally clumsy goose within a fairly strict time limit. If your only goal is to just play the game and enjoy the scenery, then you'll have a fantastic time, but if you're going for that 100% just bear in mind that there are some frustrations that will only become a serious problem once you start going for those speedrun achievements. It's a charming and silly game that was a great amount of fun, most of the time, to play. Would Honk again.

[h1] Honk If You Love Chaos — A Hilarious Must-Play! [/h1] 

Untitled Goose Game is one of the most delightfully absurd games I’ve ever played. You play as a goose — yes, just a regular goose — but with a mission: to wreak gentle havoc on an unsuspecting village. And somehow, it’s one of the most fun and memorable gaming experiences out there.

The controls are simple and intuitive, which makes it easy to dive right into causing mischief. From stealing keys and honking at unsuspecting humans to setting up elaborate pranks, the game constantly surprises with its clever objectives and comedic timing.

Visually, the game is beautiful in its simplicity. The soft color palette and minimalistic design give it a storybook feel, while the dynamic music reacts to your actions, adding a layer of playful drama to your goose antics.

What makes Untitled Goose Game so special is how it turns everyday situations into a sandbox for silliness. It’s funny, creative, and unexpectedly wholesome — a rare combination in modern gaming.

Whether you're in it for the laughs, the clever puzzles, or just to embrace your inner troublemaker, Untitled Goose Game is an unforgettable experience. Highly recommended for anyone who wants to smile while playing.

[h1]Review After 100% Completion[/h1]

[h2]Recommendation: Recommended[/h2]

[h3]What I Liked (Pros):[/h3]
+ Ran well on the Steam Deck.
+ The sheer hilarity of causing mischief as a goose, stealing hats, disrupting daily life, and honking at unsuspecting townsfolk.
+ The charming and minimalist art style that perfectly complements the chaotic gameplay.
+ Clever, open-ended puzzles that encourage creativity and experimentation.
+ Playing with my 4-year-old daughter, she absolutely adored the game, especially honking at people and stealing items. Her laughter made the experience even more enjoyable.
+ Dynamic reactions of NPCs, making every interaction feel fresh and engaging.
+ Satisfying stealth mechanics, sneaking around and causing havoc in unexpected ways.

[h3]What I Didn’t Like (Cons):[/h3]
- Some objectives can feel slightly repetitive after a while.
- Limited replayability once all tasks have been completed.
- Would have loved a few more areas or additional challenges to extend the experience.

[h3]Wishlist – Things I’d Love to See Added:[/h3]
[list]
[*]New Mischief Mechanics – More ways to mess with NPCs.
[*]DLC, New Maps or Sequel – A new location with fresh interactions and objectives, maybe a seaside village or a bustling city.
[*]Photo Mode – Capturing hilarious goose antics in detail would be great.
[/list]

[h3]Achievements:[/h3]
The achievement list in Untitled Goose Game is refreshingly straightforward and genuinely fun to complete. Thanks to the in-game notepad that tracks your objectives, most achievements feel like natural extensions of the chaos you're already causing. From stealing laundry and tormenting gardeners to locking people in garages, they all lean into the mischievous spirit of the game. But for full completion, a few standouts definitely raise the challenge level:
[list]
[*]The Pub, Quickly – Complete the pub to-do list before the church bells ring.
[*]The Back Gardens, Quickly – Complete the back gardens to-do list before the church bells ring.
[*]The High Street, Quickly – Complete the high street to-do list before the church bells ring.
[*]The Garden, Quickly – Complete the garden to-do list before the church bells ring.
[*]Pretty – Dress up the bust with things from outside the back gardens.
[*]Intrepid – Get thrown over the fence.
[*]Nimble – Score a goal.
[*]Careful – Catch an object as it's thrown over the fence.
[/list]
It’s one of the most joyfully chaotic 100% lists I’ve worked through, playful, clear, and just the right level of effort for a game that never takes itself too seriously

[h3]Memorable Quotes:[/h3]
HONK!

[h3]Final Thoughts:[/h3]
Untitled Goose Game is a lot of fun, offering playful chaos, a unique blend of humour, creativity, and simplicity. Whether playing solo or with a child, it delivers constant amusement and charming moments that make it a joy to experience. The satisfaction of completing mischievous objectives while hearing my daughter's delighted laughter made this game incredibly special. While it’s relatively short, the enjoyment it provides is well worth the time.

Untitled Goose Game: A Comedic Masterpiece of Chaos and Humor

Released in 2019 by House House, Untitled Goose Game quickly captured the hearts of gamers worldwide with its unique premise, endearing characters, and unexpected humor. The game, where players take on the role of a mischievous goose wreaking havoc in a tranquil village, stands out for its ability to make players laugh while challenging them with its gameplay mechanics. Though seemingly simple on the surface, Untitled Goose Game is a masterclass in comedy, presenting an evolving narrative that delights players with its absurdity and unpredictability. Perhaps most striking is the game's comedic ending, which turns the entire premise of the game on its head, leaving players with a grin long after they finish playing.

The Premise and Gameplay: Setting the Stage for Chaos
At first glance, Untitled Goose Game appears to be a harmless, if quirky, simulation game. Players take control of a goose who must complete a series of objectives, such as stealing items, honking at villagers, and creating general disarray. The objectives are deceptively simple but require creativity and resourcefulness to achieve, often relying on stealth, timing, and a bit of trial and error. The goose’s interactions with the environment – honking, waddling, and flapping its wings – make the gameplay feel more interactive than traditional puzzle games, creating a sense of agency and whimsy that adds to the fun.

The world is a quaint, calm English village, and the goose's behavior contrasts sharply with the serene setting. The inhabitants are unaware of the impending menace, which only makes the goose's actions more amusing. The village, with its lovingly detailed locations – from a garden to a pub to a shopping street – provides a backdrop for the goose's escalating antics. With each action, the goose disrupts the lives of the villagers in a variety of hilarious ways. The soundtrack, lighthearted yet often building to a sense of tension, heightens the sense of absurdity. As players navigate the village, it becomes clear that the primary goal is not just to complete objectives, but to do so in the most ridiculous and unexpected ways possible.

The Comedic Ending: A Perfect Conclusion to Chaos
As players progress through the game, they complete a series of increasingly elaborate tasks to cause mischief in the village. The objectives are often framed as challenges or pranks that the goose must pull off in clever ways, but it’s the game’s ending that truly stands out as a comedic triumph. The finale is a masterful blend of humor, surprise, and, of course, chaos.

In the final act, after completing all objectives, the goose has the opportunity to enter a grand, somewhat chaotic showdown with the human characters in the village. But what makes the ending so special is not just the goose's final act of mischief, but the sense of satisfaction players get from watching the absurdity unfold. The goose becomes an unexpected hero in its own chaotic way, wreaking havoc on everything from the villagers' routines to their sense of peace. The game’s conclusion is an ironic yet satisfying reflection of the journey: the goose, who has disrupted so much, is now the center of attention in a spectacular, almost cinematic final sequence.

What is most comedic about this ending is that it subverts the expectations of a traditional resolution. Instead of offering closure or a moral about the goose’s behavior, the game leaves players with a sense of giddy satisfaction. There is no dramatic plot twist or deep reflection on the nature of the goose’s antics. Instead, the ending emphasizes pure, unadulterated absurdity. The goose’s actions may seem pointless in the grand scheme of things, but therein lies the beauty of the game: the hilarity and joy derived from chaos for chaos' sake.

Moreover, the ending does not follow traditional game narrative structures. There is no villain, no redemption arc, and no deep character development. Instead, Untitled Goose Game delivers a story told through the lens of a comical antagonist – the goose itself – who acts purely on instinct. The final moments, marked by an inevitable confrontation with the villagers, encapsulate the game’s tone perfectly: a blend of mischief, slapstick, and complete unpredictability.

The Subtle Comedy of the Goose
What makes Untitled Goose Game’s comedy so effective is its subtleness. The goose never speaks, yet its actions convey an infectious personality. Every honk, every stolen item, and every deliberate misstep on the part of the villagers is both an absurd and a hilarious commentary on the unpredictable nature of life. The comedic brilliance lies in the interactions: the villagers’ reactions to the goose’s antics are often exaggerated, but their failure to deal with the goose’s chaos makes it even funnier. The game doesn’t require high stakes or serious conflict; instead, it thrives on the humorous dissonance between the peaceful environment and the raucous energy of the goose.

The goose's lack of motivation beyond pure mischief is another source of humor. Unlike traditional protagonists who have goals and desires, the goose is simply driven by the desire to mess things up for no reason other than the fun of it. This lack of any larger purpose invites players to laugh not only at the villagers' misfortune but also at how, in a world governed by rules, the goose is an embodiment of chaos without consequence. The ending, then, is the natural culmination of this absurdist tone: after all the mayhem, the goose remains untamed and triumphant, with no remorse or apology.

Conclusion: A Delightful Journey of Comedy
Untitled Goose Game is a rare gem in the world of video games, one that combines delightful gameplay with an incredibly satisfying and comedic ending. The game’s ability to make players laugh at the most unexpected moments, paired with the sheer ridiculousness of its plot and conclusion, makes it stand out as a true comedic masterpiece. The goose, as both protagonist and prankster, serves as a perfect vehicle for chaotic humor. Its antics provide endless entertainment, and the final sequence acts as a brilliant capstone to the whimsical, carefree nature of the entire experience. In the end, Untitled Goose Game is a reminder of the power of simple, well-executed comedy – sometimes, the funniest moments come from the most unexpected places.

Not Recommended | Funny idea, very slow game

Untitled Goose Game has a funny and creative concept. Playing as a goose and causing chaos is amusing at first, and the game has a nice art style that looks clean and charming. The animations and overall presentation are cool, and the idea itself is what draws people in.

Unfortunately, the gameplay quickly becomes boring. The pace is very slow, and a lot of the game involves waiting around, moving items one at a time, and repeating simple tasks. While it can be relaxing, it doesn’t stay engaging for long, especially if you’re looking for something more interactive or exciting.

The game also feels longer than it needs to be. What starts as a fun joke stretches on, and the novelty wears off before the game ends. For some players, this slow and relaxed style will be enjoyable, but for others it can feel like a chore.

Overall, I wouldn’t recommend Untitled Goose Game for most players. However, if you enjoy super chill, slow-paced games and just want something calm and silly to play without any pressure, then this might be for you. For everyone else, it’s likely to feel too slow and boring.

Honk If You Love Chaos

If you've ever wanted to embody the unholy spirit of a chaotic feathered demon with zero regard for societal norms or personal space, Untitled Goose Game is your Excalibur. You are not the hero. You are the honking, flapping, garden-invading menace your neighborhood feared in their most stress-induced fever dreams.

This game answers the age-old question: What if a goose was sentient... and also a jerk? Spoiler alert — the answer is hilarious.

Gameplay involves a to-do list that reads like it was written by a very petty goblin:

    Steal a gardener’s keys? Check.

    Lock a kid in a phone booth? Obviously.

    Ruin someone's picnic with wet bread and righteous fury? Oh absolutely.

Every task is a beautiful symphony of chaos. I once spent 15 minutes trying to drag a radio into a pond while the gardener chased me, screaming like he was defending national secrets. I failed. Then I honked and stole his rake. Victory.

The graphics are charmingly minimalistic, which is perfect, because it lets you focus on what really matters: devising new and creative ways to emotionally destabilize everyone in this peaceful village.

By the end, I wasn’t playing as a goose. I was the goose. I felt powerful. Unhinged. A little French, somehow. C'est la vie, human peasants.

Final thoughts: This game is a masterpiece of minimalist mischief. It's basically Grand Theft Auto but for birds and morally bankrupt improv comedians. 10/10, would honk again. 🪿💨

In all seriousness, this is an amazing, albeit somewhat short, game. The mouse controls were [i] interesting [/i] to get used to, but once you start playing, it makes a lot of sense and controls great. 
My first playthrough of the main campaign, with very minimal help, was only 6 hours, so don't expect a long campaign. It appears that there is a lot more post-ending content that I haven't gotten to, though.
Even though the game was short, the mechanics and subtle storytelling made it 100% worth it. This is definitely a game to enjoy the atmosphere and amazing piano music in-between your goose duties (or even when you're scheming up new plans to trick the hoomans >:3). The subtly dynamic, simple and artistic world, all on one map, all with no loading screens is a fresh breath of air, all while a large river cuts through the map, giving you a virtual fresh breath of air (and you get to touch grass [i] AND [/i] swim in water!)
As a goose, your goose duties are simply... Honk and tick people off. Some are scared, some are inquisitive, but most of them just don't want you touching their stuff... but it's so much fun sneaking around and trying to touch their stuff in spite anyways! For the first half hour of the game, I didn't exactly know what I was supposed to do, so I ended up just playing hide and seek and tormenting the first person in the game, and I was having way too much fun doing so. A part of that might just be the slightly wonky NPC AI and physics, but it's got a charm to it.

6yo Sons review:

Really good but difficult. It was hard after we competed it, getting the ball in the goal. I liked that I could play with dad, if it was 1, we wouldnt have played it because there is two of us.

Great game to play with your kid(s). It's a mischievous game full of ornery behavior, but it's all relatively harmless and simple fun. It's a nice change of pace for a game to have minor dubious objectives instead of being a destroyer of worlds. The music flows with the game depending on how you're interacting with the environment. It shifts between soft smooth pleasant classical music when you're exploring and then louder more scattery sounds when being chased. 

All in all, it's my son's (5yo) favorite game, and he's already put dozens and dozens of hours into it. Incidentally he's now getting into speedrunning and has even gotten the "Garden Quickly" achievement which I think is pretty impressive for a 5 year old.

After a hard day at work, there is nothing I enjoy more than letting out all my unchecked stress on a small child by tripping him over in a puddle of water then stealing his glasses. Now I can do it in the form of a goose without the risk of the police getting involved <3
It's kinda like low level terrorist simulator but with more replay value.

[h1] ♦️ Untitled Goose Game [/h1]
[b] Untitled Goose Game [/b] is an entertaining game that revolves around a goose terrorizing innocent civilians. Every couple years we get an indie gem like Goose Game that completely blows up out of nowhere, and I look forward to finding the next! It is a short experience that prioritizes player experimentation and never outstayed its welcome. This will be a shorter review as the game is short and relatively simple in itself, short and sweet (Just like a real goose).

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
→ The gameplay itself is not the most innovative, but that is not the focal point to begin with. It can be simplified as picking up items, interacting with items, moving the goose around, and of course honking. Through your short playthrough of Untitled Goose Game you will be set in five unique areas that all have their own secrets for you to discover. 

→ Once you’re set loose in these areas you will have a sort of ‘to-do list’ to complete. While that may sound like you’re going through the motions and just doing whatever the game is telling you to do, that is not the case. The game will set these absurd tasks like “having a picnic” or “lock the shopkeeper in the garage”. And the fun is not being told what to do, the fun is finding out how you are supposed to go about completing these tasks. This topic flows perfectly into the next section, that is the beauty of player experimentation and how well it is done in Untitled Goose Game.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2335094620

[h1] Experimentation [/h1]
→ This is what makes Untitled Goose Game the gem that it is, the exploration and experimenting to see what outcome you get is an exciting time. You have you the goose and all the perks that come with being a goose (honk!), with that and the environment you are set on a mission of terror. The world here really is your oyster, given a list of vague objectives you are tasked about how you can get these scenarios to occur.

→ The situations that occur are charming and unique, no two objectives are the same. This is really the main attribute that makes Untitled Goose Game worthy of a purchase. The game is essentially one big puzzle, and you must help the goose unravel these problems. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2335094878

[h1] Visuals & Sound [/h1]
→ The visuals in this game are stylized and further enhance the ‘indie charm’ that is already so prevalent all throughout Untitled Goose Game. Instead of going for hyper-realistic goose 4k textures we get this beautifully cel-shaded art direction. The environments here are like the cartoons you used to watch as a child and being paired by playing as a goose, it does it’s best to bring your inner child.

→ The sound direction perfectly compliments almost every aspect in Untitled Goose Game. The gameplay is wacky and cartoony, the art style is charming and cute, and is all tied together by the soundtrack. When you are exploring the town and not up to mischief the music that plays is delightful and happy, when up to no good the soundtrack quickly follows your lead and plays more intense sounds. 

→ Another welcoming surprise is how well the sounds of the environment are. Everything from a retail store door chime to a water sprinkler all have their own appropriate sounds. This really enhances the world to the next level, as interacting with the environment is a major facet in this game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2310588873

[h1] ♦️ Conclusion [/h1]
In conclusion Untitled Goose Game is a game that is perfect to play and forget about the stresses of the real world. The game offers a one of a kind experience of playing as a goose with only one thing on his mind, misbehavior. While Untitled Goose Game is an exciting and unique twist on the typical formula games feed us, I am not sure if it is a must play. The content provided is fun on its own, but what you get isn’t really worth full price. I heavily recommend that if you have interest in this game to pick it up on sale to live out your fantasies of being a goose.

[h3] Overall Score 8/10 [/h3]

When first advertised, I almost felt as though that Untitled Goose Game was just a Goat Simulator clone. Due to the Summer 2022 Steam Sale however, I got to give it more of a look before buying it. I decided to buy it and give it a whirl. The premise of the game is to complete a To-do list to get from one stage to the next. The To-do list involves puzzles being completed by way of gathering props and being a nuisance for the humans in each stage. In short, the gameplay is highly cathartic in a nonviolent way.

Aside from the wonderfully fun and cathartic gameplay, I was most impressed with the sound track of the game while you play.  It will only play at certain moments and only if the humans notice you and chase after you. For reference it sort of reminded me of the pianist expressions heard while watching the "Land of Make-Believe" sequence of "Mr Rodger's Neighborhood". Needless to say it adds a very charming personality to the game.

Untitled Goose Game is a stealth puzzle game where you play as a goose whose mission in life is to be an absolute asshole.

The controls are simple: you can honk, flap your wings, and pick stuff up with your beak. Instead of being open-ended, the game gives you a "to-do list"; most of the game is trying to figure out how to stealthily accomplish each of these tasks. The tasks are rather varied and take some critical thinking to parse out exactly what the game wants you to do.

All in all, there are 4 areas which cumulate to roughly 2-3 hours of mainline content. After you reach the credits, extra tasks will be added to the to-do list, which bump up the playtime another couple hours, if you're willing to take them on. Most of the endgame content is pretty bland by comparison (5 of the tasks are to "speedrun" the original tasklist, which I found pretty easy and repetitive), so the main game is where most of the fun is at. I didn't find the playtime to be objectionable, like other reviewers did; a simple comedy game like this doesn't need to overstay its welcome. Having said that, if you're a gamer on a budget who wants something deep and involved for your money, well frankly, I don't know why you're looking at a freaking goose game homie.

The game doesn't control well with a mouse + keyboard, so a gamepad is highly recommended. Not a big deal, but this can be annoying in multiplayer if you've only got one controller and want to use keyboard for your other player.

The minimalist art fits the premise quite well. It uses classical music (Claude Debussy) for all of its music, and though in some ways I felt like that was "an easy way out" compared to making an original soundtrack, I can't deny that it fit here nicely.

Truth be told, there's not much I can be critical about with this one. I got a few chuckles out of it, the premise never got old, and I left feeling pretty satisfied with what it gave me. I was thoroughly entertained, even if it's not the type of game that will stay in my memory for very long. Just a bit of silly fun as a goose.

What started as a funny-ha-ha meme game on the internet has certainly shaped up to be a very endearing and light hearted sandbox physics game.

Untitled Goose Game takes place in a quaint little English village, where you play as a goose who decided that today is a fine day for mischief and shenanigans, and so you set out to harass the local villagers in a variety of creative ways. You're given a laundry list of items to complete in every area in order to progress to the next area, and they involve various ways in which you annoy, scare, frustrate or otherwise bother the people around town, like hiding their tools, or locking them in, or stealing their glasses, or tripping them over, etc.

You truly get to live out your inner ***hole aspirations, and you can do it entirely consequence free, as the worst they'll do is simply shoo you away, or take back their stuff, meanwhile you can get right back to honking at them like the menace you are.

The controls of the goose are simple, maybe a bit too simple, as they tend to be a bit clunky when moving around and trying to grab things with your beak. Then again, I've never been a fan of using the mouse to move your character, so that might have something to do with it. There were several instance of me biffing a snatch'n'run manoeuvrer because the beak wouldn't connect with the item I wanted to pick up, so it did sour me on the controls a fair bit.

The game is very family friendly, as there is no violence, and there's no spoken dialogue whatsoever, and everything is relayed through body language or thinking bubbles containing images, so this is an excellent game to let kids play and have fun.

The game is also rather short, especially for the asking price. You can beat the game in about 2.5 hours, which isn't much for nearly 20€, so if you intend to pick this up at some point, I would suggest grabbing it during a sale of at least 50% off.

There are likely support groups for those personally victimised by geese out in the real world but with recent events, the ever-present threat of vicious waterfowl has all but fallen out of public consciousness. Untitled Goose Game is one of those rare golden eggs which crop up from time to time and gives the player the opportunity to fashion a feathery comeback.

For those who have been sleeping under a rock for the past year, Untitled Goose Game gleefully burst onto the scene in September 2019 after a year of social media hype, with a PS4 and Xbox One release later in December. Initially an Epic store exclusive, Steam users are finally able to get their beaks into it as the release coincides with a nifty little local multiplayer update, but more on that later.

The concept is simple, you are a horrible little goose out to terrorise a quaint British village in as many ways as possible. From the relatively simple act of dumping gardening tools into the local pond, to the complete victimisation of a particularly nervous and bespectacled young idiot, there are countless opportunities to cause mischief. A to-do list provides some necessary direction and completing tasks on the list allows progression through the linear level system, unlocking new areas to go and cause trouble in. And as far as gameplay goes, Untitled Goose Game is pretty straightforward. Your orange and white feathered menace has their versatile beak and raspy honk to use whatever objects can be found lying around, in order to achieve as much mayhem as possible. Sending villagers on —quite literally— a wild goose chase. Thinking outside of the box will often tick off secret objectives and unlock achievements, of which there are plenty.

The graphics are simple, but that all adds to its charm. The most amazing thing about this game is in the detail. From the sounds your evil avian makes as he flip-flops his way across different surfaces, to the echoes that honk back at you from a well. The attention to the small things makes this game feel polished and solid. That’s not to say there aren’t small glitches, which is to be expected from a physics puzzle game, but they aren’t intrusive and end up being a barely noticeable hiccup in what would otherwise be an excellently developed game. The soundtrack is simple yet masterfully scored, making use of classical piano compositions from Debussy which dynamically change in mood and pace depending on the situation. It unobtrusively sits in the background providing flourish and support to the rest of the game.

With the latest update, the game takes on the moniker of Untitled Geese Game allowing a second player to get in on the action locally. This opens up a ton of opportunity for collaborative scheming, and when working together seems too friendly, you can always make things difficult for your partner. You are, after all, a feathery menace to society. As an added bonus, the Steam version supports Remote Play Together, removing the requirement to be [strike]within slapping distance of your girlfriend[/strike] sat next to your player two.

From the first [i]HONK[/i] to the last, House House have packed a ton of fun into a relatively lightweight game. The price of £15 may send some gamers into a bit of a flap as Untitled Goose Game sits in the higher price bracket for a year-old casual game, but the current introductory discount reduces it to just £11 which is more than reasonable. That said, this reviewer originally bought the game on the Switch last year and loved every second and having just purchased the Steam version, remote play with distant family is now possible. A welcome distraction in the current climate for little more than the cost of a couple of coffees.

Overall, this game is definitely worth a gander. Because after all, who wouldn’t want to be a horrible little goose? 🦢

I came into this game with very little expectations gameplay wise. From the few trailers that I saw, I thought that the game seemed to have a unique style, but I never thought it would be something that I would enjoy. However, when I began to play the game, I was pleasantly surprised.
Untitled Goose Game is a fantastically structured puzzle game, charming in its nature and creative in this style. As soon as I started walking around as the goose in the first level, I immediately fell in love with this game. If you are looking for an intense game with a high level of difficulty, this isn’t the game for you because this game is very relaxed and humorous.
Weirdly, the aspect that stood out to me the most about this game is how perfectly it makes you feel like a goose. There were a number of moment where I found myself genuinely laughing and having fun playing as this goose as it terrorizes this town for its own pleasure. From the tasks that the game gives you, to the way the NPC’s react to your presence, the game does a really good job of putting you into the mind of this mischievous bird. 
Additionally, the soundtrack of this game is really excellent. Instead of having a set score play over the duration of the game, the music changes depending on what situation you are in. For example, when you are gently gliding down a canal, the piano score is peaceful and subtle. Alternatively, when you are being chased by an angry ground’s keeper, the music becomes more sporadic and spontaneous. The result is that the atmosphere of the game is consistent to the actions of the player, which further immerses you in the game. 
Every aspect of this game contributes to forming a fun and entertaining experience for the player. Despite its short length (with the initial game being about 5 hours), it still feels like it reaches its full potential and explores a vast range of creativity within its level designs. There are so many memorable moments in this game, and it was an absolute pleasure for myself to experience. I would definitely recommend this game to other people, and I think it is something that everyone should try.

[i]Untitled Goose Game (UGG)[/i]’s premise certainly captures my attention: play as an annoying goose, hell-bent on ruining the lives of normal civilians in a nearby village. Does this unique concept work out in the end? Let’s dive in.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
- Simplistic graphics that compliment the game’s tone
- Almost every object can be interacted and toyed around with
- Beautiful orchestral classical music
- Non-linear objectives that can be completed in multiple ways

[h2]Cons[/h2]
- Awkward control scheme when using mouse + keyboard
- Buggy AI makes the game frustrating

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Putting yourself in the shoes (feet?) of the eponymous goose, UGG can be described as a stealth-puzzle game. In each level/area, there will be at least one human NPC roaming around. You’ll be given a To-Do List: a series of tasks (usually annoying the NPC) that you must accomplish to progress to the next place. The difficulty of the task can range from a piece of cake to a pain in the butt. 

What I like is that the game does not hand-hold you at all. You have to figure out how to solve the tasks all by yourself, which understandably means a lot of trial and error. Most of them involve manipulating the objects around you. The goose can use its beak to grab (heavy ones can only be dragged) any object in the environment. Be careful though, the humans will not like it when you mess around with their stuff. 

The puzzles presented here are brilliant. I’ve never felt like the game had run out of creativity and become repetitive. This is helped by the NPCs having their unique quirks. For example, one area has a shy little boy that will always run away from you, thus the tasks are designed for you to scare the pants off of him. In another area, there is a burly man that will always shoo you away. Consequently, the tasks offered will encourage you to be stealthier.

Unfortunately, UGG’s basic AI can hamper your planning once in a while. For instance, if you begin piling items in one corner, away from the NPC's reach, they will begin spazzing out indefinitely until you attract their attention. Another infuriating case: if one distracted NPC stands in the way of another, they will get pushed back which can ruin your game plan. 

The control scheme here could also use a tad more polishing. The default buttons for movement are the arrow keys instead of the more comfortable WASD. I also have to bind two different keys for zooming in/zooming out because the game will not accept mouse wheel scrolls for both of them. A small nitpick, but worth mentioning.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The gist of the plot has the goose running amok, annoying the hell out of the villagers just because it can. By the end, the game reveals that there is a reason why the goose targets the place, but the story remains pretty basic. Which is okay, of course. The main selling point of UGG is the fun gameplay, not the story.

The game has a feel-good feeling to it though, as I was grinning constantly when playing it. Pranking the poor townspeople even managed to get a laugh out of me now and then. I believe the game's light-hearted tone contributes a lot to this; from the diverse colour palette to the goofy NPCs' behavior, UGG always finds a way to make you smile jovially. 

I'd also like to highlight the classical music here ([i]Préludes Complete 24[/i] by Claude Debussy, a 19th-century French composer). Every time you are pursued by someone, a piece of this music would accompany it. Surprisingly, this inclusion works wonderfully, as it makes me feel like I am in a cartoon chase scene straight out of a Looney Tunes' episode. 

[h1]Playtime, Replayability and Achievements[/h1]
[b]Playtime:[/b] It took me around nine hours to complete the game twice, accomplishing every task and getting every achievement. 

[b]Replayability:[/b] Good amount. UGG is a great stress-reliever whenever you feel tired or bored. The non-linear gameplay helps a ton.

[b]Achievements:[/b] 25 of them. Most of them are acquired by simply playing the game. The ones that are slightly challenging are probably the 'Quickly' set of achievements, which are explained in the next part.

[b]The Rest[/b]
[list]
[*] After completing the game once, a long list of hidden tasks will be revealed. These are much tougher than the base tasks, usually requiring manipulating multiple areas instead of one.
[*] Quickly Tasks is, in a nutshell, speedrunning each area as fast as possible. You have seven minutes per area before the in-game bell rings, signifying failure.
[*] Want to express your emotions as the goose? There are two dedicated inputs for that: one for honking, and another for raising your wings.
[*] A notable anti-frustration feature: whenever an object is placed out of the camera's view, a small question mark will appear in its location. This prevents players from making the game unwinnable.
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Bizarre title aside, UGG is a fun comedy game that just wants to make you laugh. It did not overstay its welcome and the puzzles are cleverly designed. Some aspects could use more polishing, but the overall product remains enjoyable. It is the perfect game to unleash that chaotic evil in you. All in all, I recommend Untitled Goose Game.

[h2] Introduction [/h2]

In the beautiful chaos that is Untitled Goose Game, players step into the feet of a mischievous goose wreaking havoc in a quaint English village. The premise is simple yet effective: it’s a lovely morning, and you are a horrible goose. Your mission? To complete a series of objectives that involve annoying and pranking unsuspecting villagers. 

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]

The controls are straightforward, allowing players to walk, honk (very important to honk a lot!) , tactical running (ducked running), and interact with various objects in the environment especially steali.. err grabbing things. The game encourages creativity as you navigate through your to-do list, which includes tasks like stealing a gardener’s hat or trapping a child in a phone booth. The interaction mechanics are designed to be intuitive; however, some players may find that controlling the goose can be slightly clunky at times. When mastering this u will be speed-running sections and waiting on the npc's to catch up,  a lot of trial and error , timed approach is key here.

[h2] Design [/h2]

The design behind Untitled Goose Game can be summarized as “simple but effective.” Each area of the game serves as an open sandbox where players can explore and execute their plans for mischief. The charming art style complements the lighthearted nature of the game-play, making it visually appealing while you engage in your chaotic antics.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

This is a delightful little puzzle game. You play the part of a goose, tasked with a list of mischief to perform. Steal the gardener's keys! Steal the little boy's eyeglasses, and then get him to find and put on a different pair that you've stolen from a shop. Steal a man's slippers off his feet as he reads his newspaper. Sneak into a TV shop and cause a commotion. Trap the shopkeeper in a garage. Honk at people right as they're in the middle of doing something delicate. Gather a list of items to make a picnic for yourself before people come to retrieve them.

There's no score, no dying, no health bar, no dialogue. Nothing but you the (genderless) goose (who can honk, flap, and waddle), the hapless townspeople just trying to go about their business, and a neighborhood full of small items to pilfer and play with. The challenge is in figuring out how to get the people into a situation where you can take things from them - and then how you can evade them so you can keep your loot. Stealth and patience are the path to success here as you waddle around trying (usually, at least) to avoid being noticed. The action is punctuated by piano doodling, sounding like an episode of Mr. Rogers' Neighborhood.

The main game, consisting of just four areas, can easily be completed in around two hours or less. Doing so will unlock more lists of mischief which require you to mix items between the areas and get the characters from different areas to interact, and there are also achievements for completing an area within a time limit. I can understand the complaint that $20 is too much for so little content, but the unlocked lists give it some replay value. It also supports cooperative two player mode; a friend can join you locally, or online with Steam Remote Play without having to own their own copy of the game (though when I tried this we had problems with lag). The game doesn't let the two geese wander very far away from each other, so it helps for both to work on one task at a time.

It's a testament to Untitled Goose Game's simple game mechanics that some people on YouTube have decided to go find what additional mischief they can get into, beyond what's asked by the lists - such as painstakingly stealing every item in the game and dropping it into the lake. You'll get no credit or achievements for this, only the sense of satisfaction that someone, in some video game universe out there, is probably putting up more signs with a picture of a goose in a circle with a line through it.

Here is one of my favourite games I have played in the past 5 years. The sheer consistency of this game is honestly baffling coming from an indie studio, because this plays better than most triple AAA games. It has a solid concept: just mess with people, which is one of the most enjoyable things you can do in real life, but this game widens the barrier to entry, due to the fact the worst these humans can do is revert your progress, as opposed to beating the piss out of you.

Untitled Goose Game is a game that gives you the full promise of its premise:  you're a goose, and your job is to [b] make everyone miserable.... [/b]that's it. [i]that's the whole game[/i]. But how you go about making everybody miserable (but in a funny way) is what makes the game so much fun and hilarious. In fact, this might be one of the most original games I've played in a long time. I mean, what other game has a dedicated HONK button? [b]GoTY  right here, man! [/b]

Hold up, before I start showering the game with unbridled praise, it'd probably be best if I got my biggest problem out of the way (and it is kind of a deal breaker): [spoiler] this game is incredibly short [/spoiler]. I beat the entire thing -including every single achievement- in about ten hours, in less than a week of owning it. I mean, the game very well knows this; as some of the achievements are basically “complete this level in six minutes or less”, and seeing how there's only five levels, it doesn't take a genius to put together and realize the game itself is saying you can beat the main campaign in less than half an hour. And all this for the price of $20? [b] Twenty dollars for thirty minutes of gameplay?? [/b] I'd recommend waiting for a sale.

Welcome to the town of... uhm... [b]Town[/b]. guess it doesn't have a name. anyway, it's a lovely little place with a population of three hundred or so. It's surrounded by beautiful forests and glades of grass and flowers; the village buildings' simple but stunning architecture is gorgeous; and it's almost like time itself moves slower while you live here. Truly, [i]Town is the closest thing we'll get to heaven on earth[/i]... oh, by the way, see that random goose over there? [spoiler]He's basically the devil incarnate[/spoiler]. yep, that's you! and your job is to make this perfect town, err... not perfect. just go out there and ruin everybody's day!  The controls shouldn't be a problem: your feathered friend will follow wherever your mouse cursor is when you left-click, while double clicking will make him run instead of walk. Right clicking next to things will either make you grab it (if it's smaller than you) or drag it (if it's your size or bigger), and right clicking again will drop whatever you're holding. Press the Ctrl key to (*ahem*)[b] duck[/b], press X to spread out your wings, and -here we go!- press space to HONK! anyway, the controls are so simple that my four year old cousin plays this all the time; so surely YOU could wrap your head around all this. The town is a big open world, split into different “levels” like Park, Main Street, and Outdoor Restaurant. You have a To-Do list for each section, and each time you cross off everything on your list, you're allowed to explore the town further. Your jobs range from mild annoyances (steal that toilet paper! honk yeah!) to...[b] some pretty dangerous stuff[/b] (trap that kid in the phone booth! honk yeah!); but no matter what you do, somebody will be made big sad. In an idea similar to [b]Ghost Trick[/b], you have to rely on NPCs in the later levels to unintentionally help you out with your tasks. You can only dress up the statue if you give the right accessories and stuff to the artist lady, for instance; and (one of) the only way to get into the pub is to hide in a box and wait for someone to unsuspectingly take you to the storage room. that's only two of many examples. There are also twenty or so special assignments on your list (that includes those time trials I mentioned before), and these can be a bit tricky. These extra jobs range from things like sailing a toy boat under a bridge, picking a bouquet of flowers, or [b]tripping a kid into a puddle[/b]. what the honk, goose? There was a particularly annoying part where you had to kick a soccer ball into a goal, but the goal was super far away AND on an uphill slope, so the ball always rolled away. I probably (*ahem*) should've called[b] fowl[/b]. anyway, Goose Game is one of those “easy to learn, difficult to master” kinds of games, but even the word “difficult” might be too much. “easy to learn, slightly less easy to master” would be more accurate.         

When it comes to production value, it's honestly impressive how Goose Game can do so much with so little. Visually, this game looks fantastic. The bright, cartoony, and rather limited color palette really makes the graphics pop; and combined with some solid (but simple) 3D and a (*ahem*) [b]birds eye view[/b] perspective, you'll be charmed in no time. Every person you meet shows tons on personality, despite having the most simplistic body features and very little voice acting (the goose is the only character with eyes and a mouth in the entire game); like how the shopkeeper is quick to anger and tries to chase you with a broom, or how the fancy man just wants to drink a cup of tea and read the paper, or how the groundskeeper is busy trying to pick vegetables. ordinary people trying to do ordinary things? [b]how utterly despicable!![/b] go ruin it for everyone, Goose!! The game has a massive variety of items you can find; slippers, candles, knives, toy cars, walkie-talkies, harmonicas, and cabbage just to name a few (THAT'S what's wrong with video games today: [spoiler]they need MORE CABBAGE!![/spoiler]). And if you don't feel like stealing stuff, you could always just waddle up to people and go HONK to see how they react. The game's soundtrack is also incredible: the only instrument is piano, but it's so energetic and zany; and the music fits so well with the action, that it's almost as if someone is watching the screen and playing the piano in real time. All of this adds up to a game with practically unlimited comedic potential; kind of feels like a classic kids cartoon forgotten by time, but then was rediscovered when everybody realized just how great and timeless the show really was. kinda gives me a fuzzy feeling, to be honest.

Aside from being extremely short, Goose Game has a couple of other issues I want to point out. none of them are crazy bad, but they still bothered me. For one, you're a goose. Geese have wings and can fly and stuff, right? But, for some reason, our pal Goose doesn't know how to fly!! worthless!!... on a more serious note, the wings aren't really used in the game at all. The spreading wings feature just feels tacked on, like “geese have wings, so Goose needs to have wings!!”, but you're only asked to use the feature once during the game, and throughout my playtime I honestly almost forgot it was a thing. Another thing, if you're being chased by somebody, and you're pushed into a wall, the result looks a bit awkward; both visually and playability. The person and the goose kind of glitch and clip into each other for a few seconds before the game irons it out. It's like the game didn't know what to do or something. Finally, and this might actually be a bigger issue than the playtime, [spoiler]the game doesn't keep track of how many times you honk!![/spoiler] like, what a missed opportunity!...no, that is straight up CRIMINAL!!

I'm just about to wrap up, but while I still have your utmost attention, let me talk about something entirely different: [b]Goose is an excellent role model[/b]. We, as people, should all strive to be more like Goose. Look at him: he doesn't judge people by superficial standards. Black or white, male or female, young or old, Goose doesn't care. [b]He hates without prejudice[/b]. and you know what? there's something inspiring about that...wait wait wait, replace hate with love, and THEN that's a nice message. nailed it.

Untitled Goose Game is an absolute joy to experience. With its unique premise, hilarious gameplay, attractive cartoon graphics, and a dedicated HONK button, it's a blast; and one of the most addicting games I've played in months. With that said, I can't deny the high price and the short playtime; but you know what? it's still worth it. well, so long... and honk honk HONK!!

A goose’s honk will trigger a fight or flight response in at least three people I know, freezing them where they stand, their fine neck hairs wispy little soldiers standing at attention, the calculus of escape crunching behind their long, glazed gazes. 

The story is the same: they were nine, at the lake with their sister and cousin, minding their business. A goose materializes from the hedge and charges, wild wings thunder like strong winds through sheets on a clothesline. Sister knocked down, shirt ripped, hair plucked out in clumps while she screams for help. Dad runs down lakeside, open-hand slaps the goose, grabs its neck, twirls thrice like a decorated discus thrower, and sends it sailing back to the hell it emerged from. The goose is not done, never done. It barrels back stronger. Dad fends it off with bows and backhands until they are up the hill to safety. 

In dreams, in perpetuity, dead beady black eyes strobe between jabs of an orange beak. God’s special little terrorist. What did we do to deserve this?

But let’s rewind a bit, play that terrible tape back again, back to the turn of the 20th century. The Canadian Goose is almost extinct, ravaged by unregulated hunting and Industry’s merciless draining of wetland habitats. Entire goose lineages downed to scattershot ends, starving, searching for a safe place to lay eggs and raise young without the specter of nature’s greatest enemy appearing in a ghillie suit on a fishing boat and leveling death itself at the riverbank, the premonition of greasy goose meat dancing on their lips.

Forward a little, conservationists and regulatory bodies acknowledge the horror we’ve wrought just at the brink of annihilation. The damage is done, but the goose is not done, never done. Federally protected, it heals quietly in what refuge it has left. In time, it will thrive again. Peace on the water, goose collectives re-emerge resolute. They will not flinch in the face of death; they will not bow before their hunter.

Forward more, back to the lake of that fateful day, three nine-year-olds milling about before the unprovoked attack. What were they doing down by that lake, one with a fifteen-pound rock raised above his head by the hedge, one skipping stones, the little girl staring serenely across the water? The roosting goose knows the visage of destruction, the devastation of its past written into its own fight or flight response. The creature with the power of flight chooses to fight.

If you were a goose, what would you call your genocide? What would you call your journey of healing? 

Untitled Goose Game puts the goose’s greatest tormentor into its webbed feet on a quest for reparations material and immaterial. Through a series of set-piece puzzles, you are tasked with unlocking doors of pastoral civilization using the only tools in your toolbox: a cumbersome waddle, a mighty HONK, and calculated mischief. Steal that farmer’s cabbage and hide his garden keys in the cabbage patch. Tie that snot-nosed kid’s shoelaces together, take his glasses, trip him face-first into a puddle. Steal that shopkeeper’s goods and sell them back to him at a premium. Stand on a grand stage and serenade picnic goers through the ancient majesty of goose song. Peck down the town until it crumbles and take what you came for.

You deserve this. They deserve this. Decades of history led to this moment of petty mischief, where we expose the triviality of human civilization and our narcissistic preoccupations, the prioritizing of our creature comforts over all while inviting the annihilation of Earth itself to our doorstep.

Set down the gun. Be the goose. Honk it out. Make humans rebuild over and again until we remember how fragile our little existence is. Apocalypse knocking, who will be left? The goose is not done, never done.

After many years, I finally bought Untitled Goose Game. To be honest, I wanted to wait until all the hype died and then I simply forgot about it.

Fast forward to today and the game still holds up.

It looks gorgeous and the sound design is fantastic with a lot of attention to details like the surface the goose is on. Story is super vague and it does not really matter. What's important here is to be a menace to everyone in the neighborhood and you do just that. The gameplay mechanics are both good and cute (honk, crouch, flap wings) and the levels are simple but fun.

It's a short game that you can beat in two hours and after you do so, the game rewards you with more tasks to do on each level you already finished although I didn't bother. I had enough and I was happy with what I got. I played this on local co-op and it was a really fun experience.

So yeah, one could say that the game is too short and that there's not enough content, but I think that if it had had more, I'd have gotten bored after a couple more levels. The game knows when to stop and I appreciate that.

It doesn't check every box on my list, but I still recommend. 8/10
