UGG is a puzzle comedy game where you play as the titular Goose. The controls are simple: left joystick controls movement as Goose makes his way through the game's small town setting. A-button allows for sprinting, B is for grabbing onto things, and X allows for honking - which is 99% for harassing and bothering the townsfolk then laughing at them. UGG is a comedy, and it is hilarious.

Each level in the game is a discrete part of the town, starting with the gardener and his garden. The player is given a checklist of different tasks that the Goose has to do in order to satisfy the comedic narrative of the game and move onto the next level.

The puzzles are clever, making sense by the game's realistic world rules. Some solutions are easier, like getting into garden, while others are more intricate, like getting the gardener wet. The human characters and their accompanying AI exclaim in "Simlish", and it's the interactions between Human and Goose that create most of UGG's humor. I don't think I've laughed out loud this much from a game, ever. Then laughed at the townsfolk by honking.

After finishing the main quest - 4 sections in all - I was delighted to find extended content for players looking for more. This could have been part of a the free DLC update that also introduced a 2-player co-op mode. This is all to say that there is a lot of good content here. Also worth mentioning is that this a great game for kids, esp. as an introduction to video games. I played it with a 7-year old who loved it!

I don't typically write reviews (particularly for games I have less than 100 hours on and have not worked towards completing achievements), but really feel I must in this case. You play as geese who cause unspeakable trauma to unsuspecting townspeople. Peace was clearly never an option. 

Pro: music was excellent and added a really special dimension. As a pianist who has played Debussy's preludes many times, it was great to see them adapted for expressive use in a video game. The music is unlike most games I play, and a welcome and refreshing change.

Con: The big con for us was the nature of the shared screen / 2-p view limited our options for chaos and generally wreaking havoc. That said, we still managed with what we had. The townspeople will curse our names for all time. 

My wife and I (neither are spectacular gamers) beat the game in ~3 hours. It was a short but fun adventure and had us laughing throughout. Highly recommend for couples who are looking for a fun, low-stress game to share together. Likely will not play through again (much in the same vein as an escape room) but recommend nonetheless. If you don't have two controllers, get them. worth it.

Such a fun, cozy and adorable game about a mischievous goose (or 2). Amazing for bonding and cooperation with family, partner or friends! I really enjoyed this. Lots of thrilling moments! 100 times more fun played together! Work together to make the whole town anti-goose 😈 One honk at a time.

Frustrations:
In couch co-op you have to fit in the same screen, which can make it difficult to move around. 
The controls are very clumsy, even on PC. Controller might actually be the better choice. You will be dropping items accidentally and having to redo a chain of events because of it. The clumsiness can be funny too, but it can get a little frustrating.
The denizens also cause you to drop items and push you, even when you're not right next to them; like an invisible obstacle. It's annoying, when trying to do a more challenging task.

The style is pretty, the goose is cute and the nature & town are charming.
The game is not very long and there are unfortunately only a couple of areas to unlock. 
It left me wanting to explore more places (for example urban and indoors; why can't I enter the houses and see what's in them? 😢). That got me looking for more possible secrets, like a route to a secret new area (which I'm disappointed not to have discovered thus far).
You can however redo the game (a couple of times?) with new lists to accomplish. First play-through took about 4 hours. Some achievements can only be acquired by replaying the areas with new goals.

The game has some puzzle elements that might leave you stuck at times.

I LOVE untitled goose game. Untitled goose game is set in a small English town. You are a goose who needs to check-off his to-do list. The to-do list will have you doing things like getting the gardener wet, stealing his keys, trap someone in a telephone both, make someone spit out there tea, make a bucket fall on someone's head, breaking the vase, ect. The game is not that big map-wise, but I just love the little town so much! from it's market on the street corner, to the outdoor pub, to it's well. I just love how the game feels so open. On top of that you have the amazing instrumental piano music that gives the game that much more personality! Untitled goose game is also 2-player local co-op, so you and your friend can wreak havoc together! The controls are pretty simple. The only thing I found the slightest hard/frustrating is a couple of the tasks, but every time you complete that one hard one it feels so good! And the few that I did find hard were not impossible nor easy, it gave me just the right amount of challenge. The game itself is not that hard, but if your looking for something too have fun with and goof around, it is PERFECT for that. The controls are simple, but they aren't the best with keyboard and mouse. I suggest using a controller, or getting it on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, or Xbox 1. Also when you "finish" the game you have a couple "to-do also" lists that add some replay ability. Overall I would say that this game is suitable for all ages, and I give this game a 10/10!

Honk honk! Welcome to Untitled Goose Game, where you play as a goose—a mean, scheming, hilarious goose—with one simple mission: ruin everyone’s day in the most delightfully annoying ways possible.

Gameplay: Mischief in Motion
In Untitled Goose Game, you’re not just any bird; you’re a havoc-wreaking feathered fiend on a peaceful village. Armed with a checklist of pranks and absolutely no shame, you’ll honk, flap, and waddle your way through a series of delightful tasks, from stealing garden tools to locking a poor kid in a phone booth. Whether you’re dragging a rake into a lake or causing a gardener to faceplant over a well-placed trap, every “objective” feels like gleeful chaos that never gets old.

The controls are honkingly simple but surprisingly strategic. Each task requires a mix of timing, cunning, and a deep, goose-like understanding of petty, feathery spite. Your tools of choice? An expertly timed honk, a sneaky waddle, and a fierce beak that can grab just about anything.

Graphics and Sound: A Pastoral Prank Paradise
The visuals? Picture book perfection! The colors are soft and cozy, with simple, hand-drawn characters that are all too easy to mess with. From the gentle blue of a pond to the warm bricks of a pub, it’s all charmingly designed to make your mischief feel oh-so-ironic. Add to that the delightfully subtle music, which swells up with each mischievous move, and you’ve got the perfect setting for goose-driven mayhem.

But the real gem is the audio. That honk! It’s the sound of pure, undiluted mischief—both alarming and hilarious. Pair it with the villagers’ bewildered shouts as they chase you down, and you’ve got an audio experience fit for a comedy show.

Honk-Worthy Highlights
Untitled Goose Game isn’t just a sandbox of slapstick; it’s a reminder of the power of simple pleasures (like stealing hats and causing general pandemonium). The freedom to creatively mess with the townsfolk is unlimited, and discovering new ways to complete tasks (or just make a mess) will keep you giggling all the way through.

Verdict
If you’ve ever dreamed of living your life as a goose, honking and flapping around without a care, Untitled Goose Game is a must. It’s a short game, but each feathered prank is a treasure that’ll leave you laughing and looking over your shoulder for future goose troublemakers.

Rating: HONK/10
In the end, Untitled Goose Game is pure, feathery joy—a simple reminder that sometimes the best games are just about causing a bit of silly, harmless chaos.

Untitled Goose Game Review: A Quacking Good Time

If you’ve ever dreamed of being a chaotic, feathered menace in a quaint English village, then Untitled Goose Game is your dream come true. This delightful indie gem lets you step into the webbed feet of a goose with an insatiable desire to wreak havoc. Who knew that flapping around and stealing people’s stuff could be so entertaining?

From the moment you honk your first honk, you’ll feel a sense of purpose. Your mission? Cause as much mayhem as possible while the poor villagers scowl in confusion. Picture this: a peaceful gardener meticulously tending to his flowers, only for you to swoop in and steal his rake, leaving him to chase you around like a scene from a slapstick comedy. It’s pure gold.

The graphics are charmingly simple, almost like a children’s storybook come to life. But don’t be fooled—behind that cute exterior lies a goose that takes joy in stealing glasses, turning on sprinklers, and dropping picnic blankets. You’ll find yourself devising elaborate plans, like a feathery mastermind plotting to trap unsuspecting villagers in your web of chaos.

The controls are surprisingly intuitive, allowing you to glide through your villainous tasks with the grace of a ballet dancer and the subtlety of a bull in a china shop. But don't get too comfortable; the villagers will fight back! You’ll quickly learn that nothing ruins your day quite like a determined human wielding a broom.

As for the soundtrack? Think of it as a delightful accompaniment to your mischief, with jaunty tunes that make you feel like a devious protagonist in a silent film. Every honk feels like a rallying cry for your fellow geese, urging you on in your quest for chaos.

In conclusion, Untitled Goose Game is a whimsical reminder that sometimes, being a jerk is just plain fun. So grab your feathers, channel your inner honker, and prepare for some good old-fashioned goose antics. Just remember, what happens in the village stays in the village—unless you leave behind a trail of chaos and stolen goods. In that case, everyone will know it was you. 🦢

Untitled Goose Game is an absolute gem that delivers pure joy from start to finish. Every moment spent as the mischievous goose is a delightful experience filled with laughter and satisfaction. The game’s charming, minimalist art style perfectly complements its whimsical nature, making it a visual treat.

The game-play is brilliantly simple yet incredibly engaging. The tasks you undertake as the goose are hilariously creative, from [spoiler]stealing a gardener’s keys[/spoiler] to [spoiler]scaring a little boy into a phone booth[/spoiler]. Each objective is a new opportunity for fun and chaos, and the freedom to approach them in various ways (for a better time) adds a layer of replayability.

What truly sets this game apart is its humor. The goose’s antics are endlessly amusing, and the reactions of the villagers are priceless. The developers have masterfully captured the essence of being a playful troublemaker, and it’s impossible not to smile as you honk, flap, and waddle your way through the quaint village.

The controls are intuitive and responsive, making it easy to immerse yourself in the role of the goose. The sound design is equally impressive, with the goose’s honks and the villagers’ exasperated sighs adding to the overall charm.

In short, Untitled Goose Game is a must-play. It’s a unique, heartwarming, and utterly entertaining experience that will leave you grinning from ear to ear. I enjoyed every moment of it and can’t recommend it highly enough!

A game so based it doesn't even need a title. Untitled Goose Game places you in control of one goose freedom fighter on a quest to rid the world of its scourge of peace, quiet and common decency. Combining stealth elements and puzzle solving, you'll swindle, gaslight and otherwise terrorize some perfectly nice people that are just minding their own business. You monster.

Being a goose isn't always easy, regardless. Advanced goose physics mean that you'll have to occasionally fight with your clumsy goose feet as you move, not to mention that the A.I. of the townspeople is unreliable and erratic, no doubt on account of your damage to their mental health. You may sometimes find your schemes thwarted by these circumstances, but don't despair! Rise above your station, and begin a new reign of chaos, at least for three hours or so. You're bound to feel better about something by the end of it!

Well, hello there, neighbors! Today, I'd like to talk to you about a delightful little game called the "Untitled Goose Game." Now, in this game, you play as a mischievous goose who's out and about in a peaceful village, causing all sorts of silly antics.

What I love most about this game is how it encourages kindness and empathy, even as you're causing a bit of chaos. You see, as you waddle through the village, honking and causing a ruckus, you're also helping people in your own playful way. Whether it's bringing a smile to someone's face by stealing their hat or simply spreading joy with your silly antics, there's a sense of warmth and whimsy that permeates every moment of gameplay.

And oh, the joy of discovery! As you explore the village, you'll find all sorts of hidden nooks and crannies just waiting to be explored. From lush gardens to bustling shops, there's always something new and exciting to uncover.

But perhaps what I love most about the "Untitled Goose Game" is its message of embracing our playful side and finding joy in the little things. It reminds us that even in the midst of our busy lives, it's important to take a moment to laugh, to play, and to spread a little kindness wherever we go.

So, if you're looking for a game that's sure to bring a smile to your face and warmth to your heart, I wholeheartedly recommend giving the "Untitled Goose Game" a try. After all, who wouldn't want to spend a day in the shoes of a mischievous goose, spreading joy and laughter wherever they go?

Charming minimalist puzzle game that will make your creative juices flow. The entire game is very short, just 4 main 'quests' (to-do lists) which can be finished in a single sitting. Controls are tight and responsive, which helped me to focus on solving the puzzles. Game mechanics are pretty simple, as you primarily interact with the world through your beak. Difficulty is well-balanced—neither too hard nor too easy. Engaging yet not too intensive, I'd say that this title is perfect for backseat gaming or 2-player mode where you can play and chat with people at the same time. Highly recommended if you can pick this up for a sale.

Well I am glad I gave this game a chance, years after it came out, when I had forgotten about it - I thought it was a typically pretentious-arty indie game all in the looks and style and not in the content... I was wrong.
Instead of explaining why I came back to it, or giving a long review, I will just give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar: do you guys know SovietWomble? This youtuber/twitcher hilarious man is mostly for his old CS/Arma funny videos (I recommend watching some), but he also has amazing insight on games (The Forest etc). He recently did a short video on this game: if you are ok with spoilers (and if you are not just watch like the first few minutes or so), watch his video, THEN you should know like me if you are intrigued by this game or not. For me, watching the pure joy and fun SovietWomble had while playing this game (admittedly, probably narrating to his chat) was enough to tell me I HAD to try this game too. And I am glad I did! This game is indeed a bit arty but not very pretentious and most of all it is totally meaningful and smart in its design. I LOVED every second of it.
Be a naughty, silly, stubborn goose and mess around, discovering dozens of way to annoy people, to do cheeky, nasty tricks with their lives and their belongings... messing around just for fun could be enough for some, but I want more, and I am glad the devs added objectives, which, very ingenuously, unlock the path to the next area once completed! So smart.
I am about to finish the game at 100% (my ruined hand won't allow me right now) just to say thank you to the devs, as their game is very witty and well written. The narrative, almost whimsical loop of the whole thing makes it even smarter and laudable. And most of all... that goose is so cheeky and adorable.

I will keep this short as I believe anyone that might wish to get this game will get it regardless, and those who don't, won't.

A lovable cute art style; consistent throughout and easy to the eyes.

A satisfying sound design.

Simple but cathartic gameplay loop (get the things, mess with people, escape).

And the simple extra challenge of all that but on a timer.

This game is at its absolute best with a friend, but a decent time-killer on your own.

What else can I say?  There is a honk button and you are a goose, and your friend is a goose too if you're playing co-op.  A wonderful little gem made with love.  It knows what it wants to be, it is what it wants to be, and it's exactly the kind of game one might play on a fifth date or something.  Love it.

In concept and in viewing, it's quite funny. However, playing the game yourself? Not so much. The controls... are a lot left to be desired. Turning is abysmal whether you're running or not, running feels very clunky (Not to mention you have a hard time actually getting away from the people if they're chasing you, and it have a lower turn control definitely doesn't help), and picking up some objects is more trouble than it's worth. Don't forget, you can softlock yourself by putting the bell in the garage and closing the garage, only to find out you can't open it. So what ends up looking like a good spot while you're surveying the market area ends up screwing you over and that late into the final task. And while it's funny at first (the game, I mean), it really does just devolve into headache-inducing puzzles that you need a guide for because some are just that convoluted, like making the burly guy get a bucket on his head or stealing the gardener's hat. Coupled with the game's controls make for what looks like a meme game turned into an infuriating experience. Unfortunate, too, because conceptually, it's a great idea. It's just the execution has a lot to be desired for.

I'm 48 years old and have been a gamer all my life, starting back with the Atari 2600, then Commodore 64 and on to the present. I've played the greats: from Pac-Man to Half Life to XCOM to Minecraft to...you get the idea. It's a long list.

This game is in my top 10. I play with my six-year-old son and we laugh so hard we almost fall out of our chairs. Even my wife watches and cackles. The missions are fun puzzles and--even outside of those--it's fun to just annoy the ever-living s**t out of the villagers.

That said, some of these missions seem like they would be really difficult without two people. It originally released as single-player so it must be possible. I guess you could use the walkie talkies (yes, you can find walkie talkies and it's f-ing **hilarious**). 

You can't rotate the camera, and sometimes an object will go out of view. A question mark icon will appear at its location, and you can pick up almost everything except round objects--of which there aren't many. I think this is by design as I'd call it faux-3D. Being able to rotate the camera would detract from the charm IMHO.

There was one time we had to reload. We'd locked the farmer out of his garden, but the keys were inside the gate. We hadn't unlocked the area to where we could go around. Fortunately, as far as I can tell, the game auto-saves after you achieve each objective.

Buy this game, especially if you have someone to play with.

[h1]Overall Impressions[/h1]
Reviewed after 100% completion. A unique, relaxing puzzler with a funny protagonist and a sense of style. 

[h1]What I Liked[/h1]
This game is charming, has tight controls and doesn't overstay it's welcome. It is also such a relaxing game. After a stressful day, it felt great to unwind on the couch, steam deck in hand and try to casually figure out the puzzles for each area while the piano tunes played in the background. I never felt stressed out. 

[h1]What Could Be Improved[/h1]
It does have a co-op mode, but I found it to be more of the solo experience but with the option for another Goose. While I appreciate the inclusion, there wasn't a whole lot of specific two-player type puzzles.

[h1]Final Thoughts & Rating[/h1]
Untitled Goose game is like nothing else I've played. It has a keen sense of style and self-knowledge and doesn't try to stray too far from what makes it great. Highly recommend if you're looking for a relaxing game.

[b]Sights & Sounds[/b]
- With simplified features, smoothed textures, and muted outlines that combinr to make the 3D world look like a cartoon grew by a dimension, I thought for a while that this was an Annapurna game. Maybe that's just because I've played both Virginia and Donut County
- I still do like the art style, though, even if it's not totally unique. What stands out more than that is the animation, specifically the way your goose moves. The waddle is especially eye-catching and silly, enhancing the humor of your antics
- The soundtrack is the game's composer's own arrangement of Debussy's Preludes, so I hope you like classical French music. I thought it served as a pretty nice auditory backdrop to all the shenanigans

[b]Story & Vibes[/b]
- You're a goose. All geese are inherently evil. Ergo, your job is to unleash your hatred upon a cozy little town, giving form to your spite and leaving destruction in your wake
- It probably won't be a surprise to hear that the overall tone is overtly silly and lighthearted

[b]Playability & Replayability[/b]
- Your controls for ruining everyone's day include abilities to drag/pick up objects, flap your wings (menacingly!), duck your head, and, most importantly, honk
- At the beginning of every new area you waddle into, you're given a checklist of things to do, most of which are pretty funny. After completing a certain number of them, a new to-do item will appear. Finishing that final task will open the door to the next area
- I won't spoil the game's final task, but it's fun and frantic
- At its heart, Untitled Goose Game is a puzzle game with occasional steal mechanics, but it somehow feels more like a toy than a game in a way I really appreciated
- I played the game in couch co-op with my wife. I appreciated that the ability to zoom the camera in and out gave us the freedom to focus in on puzzles that needed our attention, but still move to a wide shot to spread out if we were completing two different tasks at the same time

[b]Overall Impressions & Performance[/b]
- Having tried this in both single player (on the Switch some time ago) and now again in multiplayer, I'd really recommend the co-op experience. It was really fun to do things like run distraction while my wife swiped the gardener's radio or steal a kid's glasses after she tied his shoelaces together. Crime is more fun with a partner
- It's a little indie title, so you won't have much trouble running this on anything. I think it's verified for the Steam Deck as well
- I didn't notice any bugs or run into any issues, but this seems like the sort of game that may get softlocked by an item becoming unreachable

[b]Final Verdict[/b]
- [b]7.5/10[/b]. Consider this a rating for the multiplayer experience; it's still a worthwhile game for a solo playthrough, but maybe half a point less enjoyable

🦢 Untitled Goose Game 🦢

My friends, today I want to give you a candid review of Untitled Goose Game, an experience that made me laugh and frustrated me at the same time. As a goose, this game is a masterpiece for me!

🌟 Beautiful Rabbits and Malicious Geese

In the game, you look like a cute rabbit. But you are actually a malicious goose! Your mission is to ruin people's lives in a quiet English village. Yes, you heard that right. You deal with simple but fun tasks like chilling people's tea, stealing garden statues, and stealing laundry.

🎭 The Secret Life of a Goose

The best part of the game is to see how amazed people are when they see you. They open their eyes wide and think, "What is that goose doing?!" That's when the heart of the little malicious goose inside me beats fast. 🙃

🔔 Challenges and Triumphs

Gaming can be frustrating sometimes. You can spend hours trying to complete a mission. But when you finally succeed, that feeling of victory is really satisfying. "Yes, people! I'm a goose and I've taken over this garden!" you want to shout.

🌈 Visual Art Wonder

The graphics are simple but magical. The color palette and environmental design draw you in. It feels great to wander through a world filled with the beauty of the English countryside.

🎶 Soundtrack and Sound Effects

The soundtrack is light and cheerful. At the same time, the environmental sounds perfectly reflect the atmosphere of the game. Especially the "goose screams" during the human chase are my favorite!

All in all, Untitled Goose Game offers an extraordinary gaming experience. It's fun, funny and a little bit crazy. If you want to be a bit crafty and surprise people, this is the game for you. 🎮🌟

Untitled Goose Game is pretty clearly a meme-y game. The problem is telling when highly rated meme-y games are actually good, and when people just recommend them because of the meme. Thankfully, Untitled Goose Game is actually a good game. It’s not very long or complex and it doesn’t have the best graphics, but it is fun. You basically do exactly what the description says. You’re a goose and you cause chaos by completing tasks or creating your own fun messing with the AI. The AI is quite reactive to the things you do, which is what makes the game good. Quite simply, messing with this AI is fun and I’m glad I decided to give this game a try, even if it only took me 3.5 hours to seemingly do everything except the speedrun challenges. It would have been nice to have a few more levels, but I am still happy with my purchase.

Also, this seems like a perfect game to have Steam Trading cards and Steam Point Store items for profile customization, so it would be nice to see that stuff added.

I recently had the immense pleasure of diving into the quirky world of the "Untitled Goose Game," and let me tell you, it's an absolute gem that will leave you grinning from ear to ear. This delightful masterpiece of mischief and mayhem is a testament to the creativity and wit of game developers. This game lets me channel my inner goose self and love for annoying people and stealing shoes.

From the moment you waddle into the shoes (or should I say webbed feet?) of the mischievous goose, you're in for a treat. The game's charming visuals, coupled with its playful soundtrack of different piano notes, set the stage for an adventure that's as heartwarming as it is hilarious. The attention to detail in the game world is astounding; every nook and cranny is filled with opportunities for mischief, and you'll find yourself cackling with glee as you terrorize the unsuspecting villagers.

What truly sets the Untitled Goose Game apart is its intuitive gameplay mechanics. Controlling the goose feels natural, and the puzzles are cleverly designed, encouraging you to think outside the box to achieve your feathered objectives. The joy of honking at just the right moment or stealing a villager's hat without them noticing is unparalleled.

But beyond its gameplay brilliance, the game's real charm lies in its ability to evoke a genuine sense of happiness and amusement. It's impossible not to crack a smile as you watch the chaos unfold, and the interactions with the villagers are both endearing and comical. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, and that lighthearted approach is infectious.

In conclusion, the Untitled Goose Game is a triumph of creativity, offering a joyful and refreshing experience that will leave you feeling elated. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or just looking for a fun way to unwind, this game is an absolute must-play. Prepare to embark on a feathered escapade like no other – one that will leave you laughing, honking, and thoroughly entertained. Bravo to the developers for crafting such a whimsical masterpiece!

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

You might remember this from the ‘peace was never an option’ meme a few years back. 
Untitled Goose Game (UGG) is surprisingly fun. Be a goose, be out to ruin the day of everyone in the village, honk, chase, steal, and manipulate your way to victory.  It is surprisingly cathartic and cheeky. 


[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The art style is stripped back, but quaint. It fits the theme nicely and possibly gives the goose more character in doing so.  
[*] The goose can honk, spread its wings, and its movements appear enjoyably gooselike. 
[*] The human reactions are surprisingly gentle given your shenanigans, mostly gentle shooing and complaints. It’s nice to have a game about being a pest that doesn’t get you killed every 5 minutes. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Quite short. While it helps maintain the peaceful nature of the game, I almost never give thumbs up for games that cost more in pounds than provide hours of playtime. 
[*] Goose control via mouse and keyboard is quite strenuous and can be very irritating. A lot of clicking and holding, even with toggle turned on its hard to get it quite right. This game feels very much like it’s built around, and optimised for, a controller. 
[*] The challenges are quite samey. Again, the short nature of the game means they don’t get all that old, but the lack of variety or changes can be seen clearly in how 50% of the people who took the time to complete the first level then didn’t both finishing the game, which took a single evening to play. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] I paid half price for this, and I would say I over paid for it by half again. Pull the cost down to reflect the product.
[*] More optimisation for keyboard and mouse. 
[*] A flappy jump. 
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]

This game is fun. 
It’s not for people out to kill things, or who want fast paced action. It’s not really a for hardcore puzzle enthusiasts either, given the simplistic nature of the game. 
This game is for casual gamers for sure. It’s for people looking for a peaceful break from their usual game genres. 

Really, UGG is a little bit for everyone, you just need to be in the right space for it.

I played through the game co-op with my sister. It was a loooooot of fun to be a couple of sassy geese going around ruining people's day. We laughed often because the concept, art and gameplay are so charming. It's also quite rewarding when you can figure out how to accomplish the less obvious tasks.

You can interact with pretty much everything and do all kinds of things to bother the villagers. You can do plenty of things that have nothing to do with anything, which added an interesting element to co-op.

The reason I add that it's "frustrating" at times is that the controls were not the smoothest (rounding corners quickly is not easy and we kept getting stuck on things). I wouldn't say that's a deal breaker - we just laughed about it or swore at the screen and moved on. While it can interrupt you from accomplishing a task, it just resets a bit and you can try again. 

Once you play through the main checklists, new tasks open up to you that bring the different areas together. It's also a different experience playing solo than with a friend, so you could have more than one run-through that way.

Overall I definitely recommend! If there's a sequel or if this becomes a series of games, I will definitely be playing more!

[b]"Untitled Goose Game" allows you to be an evil goose that makes a mess whenever it goes. It sounds weird, but delivers some really entertaining time. It's visually beautiful with fluid animations, natural physics, smooth controls and adorable music. The tasks that you have to accomplish are well designed and offer some refreshing gameplay mechanics. It would be nice if there was a story to give you a reason of doing things though. Occasionally it may look like just another silly, troll game, but It manages at least to transform being a goose into a hilarious experience. 


Manometer: 7/10[/b]


The good
- Beautiful aesthetics. Minimal, cartoonish graphics with nice chromatic palette. It looks so clean, but also has some cool details here and there.
- Awesome, fluid animations. Goose's movements, how it walks, how it grabs things or pulls bigger ones with more effort, everything looks realistic and eye pleasant.
- It has some pretty cool tasks that look like small puzzles. They're pretty simplistic, but they have fun and offer some interesting and refreshing gameplay mechanics. Most of them get solved in multiple ways. There are some extra, a little bit harder, tasks even after finishing the main game.
- Smooth, responsive controls. Being a goose was never so immersive.
- Great physics and collisions. Each object behaves differently depending on its weight and center of balance. Friction when pulling or pushing things looks good. Things dropping and knocking each other is realistic enough. 
- Much interactivity. You can grab and move almost everything that is close to goose's size. This makes its world feel more alive and immersive.
- Nice minimal music that fits perfectly to visual aesthetics and enhances the overall humorous vibes.
- It's hilarious. The concept of being an evil goose that makes a mess wherever it goes is funny, but it gets even better by the NPC's reactions, their frustration and goose's honks. 

The bad
- There is no main story or a profound reason of doing things. I know you're just a goose, but it has to give you a purpose. Now, you do random tasks just because an list of objectives tell you so. After a while messing with everything aimlessly may feel monotonous and a bit silly.
- NPCs' AI is mediocre. They have short repetitive routines, slow reactions and you can easily trick them. They are allowed to move inside certain boundaries so you can get away pretty easily. Yeah, it isn't a stealth assassin simulation game, but its gameplay is based on how you deceive people so AI should be better.
- Cameras are occasionally problematic and things can get hidden behind others. It would be nice if you could rotate the camera freely and zoom out more.

Fun little humorous game in which you are an annoyance to people and have to outsmart them in certain situations. Would be more enjoyable if the controls weren't so horrendous, no matter what you set them to (mouse+keyboard). Makes for very clunky movement.

Stupid honk memes aside, this game is an exercise in frustration.
Want to put items in a shopping basket for a quest? Too bad, the shopkeeper sees it from MILES away and undoes your progress.
Accidentally fell into the river while trying to drop a glass in it and forgot to open a shortcut door, which only opens from one side? Too bad! Have fun slooowly going through the whole map to get back to this location.
Finally got to the last quest? Have fun carrying an item that immediately attracts attention to anyone, and more so if you sprint! And you have to wrestle it back everytime you drop it. Oh, and did I mention that all the shortcuts you could use to speed this up are magically patched up just for this quest?

Maybe it wouldn't be so bad if the controls were good. The default KB/M controls are complete trash, even when I switched from mouse to arrow keys, it didn't help. Controller is a bit better, but still not good. If the walk/sprint was not wonky, if you didn't have to move to a specific position to take an item off of people's hands, the game would be so much better. Instead, you have to wrestle both the controls and the NPCs. It's only funny when your progress gets undone maybe a couple of times, but it happens constantly.

Hard pass.

one imagines the untitled goose game to be simple in nature, yet it is far from. as one continues throughout the adventure of this mischievous mallard, they gain a sort of appreciation for its complexities. coming from someone recently engrossing themselves in this journey, i can wholeheartedly back up this claim. whether its your first time through, just completing the core objectives and exploring the four diverse regions, or finding the secret tasks, ones much harder, its clear that untitled goose game is great.

typical to many indie games, this treasure was clearly well polished and carefully designed. the way that they designed the game in a way that is obviously 3D, but cleverly put in a perspective of 2D style gameplay was a breath of fresh air from the usual one or the other. untitled goose game as a whole is lovely; the art style: magnificent, the soft piano music: beautiful, the interactions made with the npcs: hilarious at times.

my only gripe with the final product is the achievements, more specifically, the "___, quickly" set. to complete these achievements and 100% the game, each area has to have its tasks done in less than seven minutes. for this to happen, you must find a route that allows for quick task-doing, while avoiding the finicky movement of npcs and grab mechanics. even then, it could be imperfect, and the tasks might be done right after the bell strikes. when this happens, its time to restart and try again. this, without a doubt, was the worst experience, especially the back gardens.

in summary, the untitled goose simulator is not perfect, it can be at times one of the most frustrating things available on steam, and at others you feel like you are on top of the world. my time playing this was a mix of these things, and i overall had a wonderful time. house house made a masterpiece, but one not everyone can understand.

A fun, low stakes stealth game that rewards you for terrorizing people, messing with the environment and prodding your way into places you shouldn't be.

The presentation and (dynamic/reactive) music remind me of kids' cartoons from when I was little (late 90s and early 2000s, mostly PBS ones I think) which is an interesting dash of nostalgia.

The areas have a good sense of escalation to them, and each one has interesting character behaviors to discover and exploit. In a way, this game feels like it takes the least violent parts of the Hitman games and fleshes them out. If exploiting a variety of human quirks and pet peeves to break into new and more complicated areas sounds interesting to you, this game definitely has something for you.

I finished the game, and all of the bonus tasks/time trials at my current playtime as of writing this review. If ~6.5 hours for full completion seems low for a $20 game, I gotta say, it feels longer than that when you're playing, in a good way. I've got good memories of my time playing through it, and the extra tasks and time trials reward clever thinking and familiarity with the areas; they're very rewarding.

I'll add that I don't think playtime is everything when it comes to the price, and this is another one of those games where the experience and good memories you can make with it is worth more than just how many hours you can sink into it. I say that as someone who enjoys a good time sink every once in a while, too.

(I never messed with the co-op anyways, if you have a friend to play with I'm sure you can get even more of your money's worth, if it still concerns you)

I started playing this game alone, and I was not expecting a puzzle game. Some of the puzzles are quite difficult with only one person! They're also challenging with two people, but I think it's way more fun to play with someone else. I brought on my younger brother as my player 2 and it was super fun to complete some shenanigans together. Very cool game - we only have the bonus quests left!

While I'm sure that $20 worth of effort went into the game, there's not $20 of content. I bought it for $10.59 on sale, but if I were to set my own price I probably would have paid $5. I'm not going to try and return it because I can afford to overpay for entertainment, but I was genuinely surprised that the game ended where it did. For a twenty dollar game, I was expecting content along the lines of Kerbal, Factorio, or Subnautica. In hindsight I realize now that I got those games in early access, that those games in particular may be exceptional in terms of content and quality, and that $20 just isn't what it used to be. The "overwhelmingly positive" reviews don't really reflect the lack of content either, and I get the feeling a lot of it is from meme reviews leaving a positive review to say: "goose game funny." And, no offense people, but I get the feeling that a lot of you got it for the memes and never completed the puzzles. So in all seriousness, and from someone who completed the main game: find a different puzzle game for $20. 3.7 hours, even 3.7 good hours, just doesn't cut it.

It's a small, charming, well animated and sometimes vapid game.  It's can be kind of frustrating when its own simplicity works against it.  When you are given such a simple world and simple activities, it can be frustrating to fight against a simple game to complete a simple task.  I'm also not sure how much fun the game is to play for yourself, versus an audience.  Like, this is the quintessential *watch me play* game, as without someone to enjoy the irreverence with I'm not sure it really holds up moment-to-moment.  It really is the type of experience you want to share with others.

Nevertheless, it works.  It's a nice break from "standard gameplay loops" and skill-based activities you would see elsewhere.  It's a nice evolution of the walking simulator, elevated by basic gameplay features, visual puzzle solving and a dedicated honk button.  It's fun to be a goose for a little while.

I guess I was expecting this to be more of a sandbox game and less of an explicit puzzler. There's benefits and drawbacks to both approaches. The sandbox approach would risk boredom, and without being given any direction I imagine it might become frustrating not knowing how many reactions or outcomes one is missing out on by not having discovered the proper triggers for them. Conversely, the puzzle solving approach encourages and allows for more complexity in setting up elaborate, multi-step pranks that an individual player would likely never stumble upon without at least some guidance; but it also imposes a certain amount of linearity, and dampens somewhat the joys of pure discovery and anarchic-ness.

I was immediately disappointed when the checklist first made it's appearance at the start. (A meddlesome goose with a [i]to-do list??[/i] The scourge of productivity strikes again!) Realistically there was probably no other way to make this work, and any alternative would have likely ended up less fun. To their credit, they also do a good job trying to encourage more aimless experimentation by way of the "To Do (As Well)" secret checklist, whose items are only revealed after they've already been accomplished (or once the main game is beaten).

I also try to remind myself of a phrase my old professor, the filmmaker Thom Andersen, liked to repeat: "suspense is an alienation effect." In other words: by prolonging narrative closure, raising a question and then leaving it unresolved for a certain period of time, you create a space of heightened attention for the viewer, and this attention can be re-directed however the director sees fit. (Andersen's favorite example of this was a scene in the 1973 political thriller [i]The Day of the Jackal[/i] where otherwise mundane Parisian street scenes become strangely riveting by virtue of our knowledge that Charles de Gaulle's would-be assassin is hiding somewhere among them.)

There is a case to be made that an analogous principle exists in game design: goals are an alienation effect. The gap between assignment and execution opens up its own space of unresolved tension, heightening our perception, and—in a feature that distinguishes games from a medium like film—directing or guiding our behavior. The experience of the game, in other words, is what happens while we're busy trying to accomplish other plans.

Still, there's part of me that laments the narrow way that goal-oriented engagement hews and anchors our attention. How much of the game's world is blinkered out as I fixate on solving the problems it presents me with? How much is lost when I perceive that world as purely means to various ends? How does the pleasure of an action done for its own sake compare to the satisfaction of an action within a chain leading to an end result already known in advance? (Even the attempt to uncover a "hidden" objective creates a wholly different, and arguably impoverished, way of looking from that of open-ended playfulness.)

I'm reminded too that Thom Andersen, in addition to his love for classical narrative cinema, is one of the most notable critical champions of the filmic work of Andy Warhol. Perhaps that's what I wanted out of this. A more Warholian experience. Not the heightened mundanity transformed by the alienation effect of suspense/objectives, but mundanity itself, raw. A slab of time to live in. An array of objects and effects and patterns to fuck around with.

But I suppose at that point what I'm asking for isn't really a [i]game[/i] at all. So I can't say I was misled. After all, it's right there in the title.



[i][b]Someone on Backloggd commented on this review to ask me "what I thought about how the game actually did what it was going for" – so here was my response to that...[/b][/i]

I thought it was amusing, relaxing, pretty to look at, not a bad way to spend a few hours. I appreciated how the map opening up as you progressed was handled (lots of clever linkages between areas, created indirectly by your actions in unexpected ways). And I thought the way the end of the game circled around to the beginning was elegant and satisfying. Some of the mechanics of how the puzzles were solved felt arbitrary. (i.e. If you pull out the stool from under the old man at moment A he turns around and sees you, but if you do it at moment B he falls on his ass. Why? Because that's how the AI was programmed.) It's ultimately a game about observing behavioral patterns and then manipulating those patterns to create a window of time and space to do what you need to do. I liked the stealth elements, and thought it was funny that they directly reference [i]Metal Gear[/i] by requiring you to hide in a box in one segment. The ability to flap your wings was never really utilized, which felt like a missed opportunity.

If we're talking consumer review perspective: it felt like a rather paltry amount of content for 20 bucks.

One of the best things about Untitled Goose Game is its sandbox-style gameplay. The game takes place in a small village, and players are free to explore and cause trouble at their own pace. The game is full of clever puzzles and challenges that players must solve in order to progress, and the solutions are often hilarious.

The game's controls are simple and easy to learn, making it accessible to players of all skill levels. The goose can honk, flap its wings, and use its beak to pick up and interact with objects in the environment. The game also has a great sense of physicality, and players will need to use the goose's abilities to navigate the world and solve puzzles.

Overall, Untitled Goose Game is a clever and charming game that is sure to put a smile on your face. It's a great game for players of all skill levels, and it's a refreshing change of pace from more traditional video games. If you're looking for something fun and different to play, this is definitely a game to check out.

Mixing stealth with hilarity with the deep, often ignored, dark human lust for chaos and bullying small children. This game has a surprisingly beautiful ending and tells a charming tale while leaving much up to the players interpretation. It manages to have replayability while still having a good storyline that is satisfying every time. It also has a fun interactive soundtrack that gives cues and clues in game. The game is puzzling enough to be difficult but not impossible. The instructions are clear enough that you know exactly what you need to do, but vague enough you aren't sure how to do it. Each level has at least one difficult problem that you have to think outside the box for, and always you must look around for what to do. The bonus content (extra lists) at the end of the game offer even more replayability, during which I guarantee you will find easter eggs and little things you didn't notice before. The lists often have one clear way to do things, but you can always do it another way, so I strongly recommend looking outside the box for strange ways to do things when replaying, it almost always pays off. I waited over a year to the release of this game. I did not wait in vain.

Some eagerly anticipated things turn out to be less than they were promised to be. For UGG this was impossible, because the bar was so low that nothing could go wrong. You control a horrible goose, and you have to figure out ways to torment the residents of a village one fine morning.

The sound design, like the art and actual gameplay, is charmingly minimalistic, mainly consisting of a piano score that syncs to the action and sounds reminiscent of Johnny Costa. There's no dialogue or story to worry about; this is a situational puzzle game where the objectives are to be a jerk in creative ways and to accomplish certain non-trivial acts of sabotage. How you accomplish these things, and how long they take you, are matters left to you as the player. As is the amount of honking your goose does.

If you liked Wingspan, that doesn't necessarily mean you'll love this. But you should get it anyway, and nobody's paying me to say that. Really, I mean it. I was not paid to make this endorsement.

As much as I think the game is very charming, I would not buy this game at full price. I bought two copies of the game, one for myself and another for my friend so that we could play multiplayer, but I found out too late that there is no online multiplayer, only local. We played for 5 hours on my friend's copy, hence why my playtime is so low. We completed the main campaign and all but two of the bonus objectives ("score a goal" and "get tossed over the fence"), and didn't bother with any of the time challenges. Minor spoilers below (objects, locations, but not solutions to puzzles).

The controls are not very responsive (although that could also be chalked up to being part of the goose simulation), which is why we could not bring ourselves to completing the game even though it is relatively short and enjoyable. Trying to get the goose to go in the right direction (without sprinting, since I am aware sprinting makes turning harder) is downright painful, and makes many of the challenges much more annoying to the player than the NPCs (when the whole point of the game is to cause trouble for the NPCs).

I'm also not a fan of how object locations are not saved, because part of the fun my friend and I had made was collecting objects and bringing them back to the bell stash. We had collected all the flowers, all the anti-goose signs (except the chalk sign in the marketplace because that one is not draggable), and many other miscellaneous items from each area before we had to take a break, and upon reloading the save we found our stash was gone. I know this is probably to prevent the player from softlocking themselves out of an objective, but it did lead to us feeling like we were just checking boxes and not actually having an impact on the town. The best part of the mischief is leaving a lasting trail of carnage everywhere you go, and objects resetting destroys that feeling.

I also didn't like how there was no splitscreen option for the multiplayer, but rather the two geese cannot be too far from each other. This may be a balancing issue, as being able to have one goose lure an NPC away while the other goose does mischief could make certain puzzles much easier, but still it was really annoying to be trying to sneak around an NPC only to be stuck in place because the other player is too far away. This was especially notable in the pub where the burly man can chase one goose out of the pub and force the two geese far apart, leading to lots of finagling to get the geese together so they can move again.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Untitled Goose Game is the quirky indie game that AAA studios just can't make anymore. In this game you play as the titular goose running, honking, and flapping your wings through a suburban English village. The game sees you navigate through four scenarios, a garden, a street, two interconnected backyard gardens, and a pub. These four settings are seamlessly connected as you complete a "to-do list" of puzzles and tasks involving collecting or placing props in the interactive environment and having human NPCs react with them in fun and unique ways. One thing that should be noted is this is an extremely short game, about four hours in length, including the hidden "to-do list" and speed-run challenges, but even so I believe it's worth the $20 price tag.

This is probably the best game I have ever played. Being a goose is a wonderful experience that I think everyone should have at some point in their life. Especially when you are a goose who likes "shiny" things (my definition of "shiny" is like "Oooooooo, what's that?" and not "Wow. That sparkles in the light", although sparkly things are also "shiny" things in my opinion). Playing this game makes me feel like I AM the goose. And that goose makes me feel like a crow. I love crows! I also love geese. Crows in general and this goose have a lot in common. They look great in bow ties of any color, they like shiny things, and they make funny sounds. (They are also both birds, but that's besides the point.) Also, the music is amazing, the art is amazing, the characters are amazing- I've given all of the characters their own backstories at this point. I REALLY recommend this game. When I first read about [I]Untitled Goose Game[/I] back in 2019, I admit I was skeptical of its potential. Just how fun could a game about a malicious goose that pesters citizens of an idyllic English village be? Well, as it turns out, it’s a lot.

[I]Untitled Goose Game[/I] didn’t capture my interest until I learned from watching a Let’s Play video from classical violinist/comedy duo, TwoSet Violin, that the game’s soundtrack features excerpts from Claude Debussy’s [I]Préludes[/I]. Seeing the unexpected mix of anatine shenanigans and classical music, I knew I had to give this game a chance.

Do I feel daft about my initial skepticism! [I]Untitled Goose Game[/I] is a really good game! It’s surprisingly challenging, at times trying, unpredictably funny, and absolutely joyful. The traversable space of the village is divided into five major areas, with each having its own list of mischiefs to tackle. Figuring out how to carry out these shenanigans is the focus of the game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791350764

The village may be small, but it’s a well-designed setting for causing plenty of trouble. This makes discovering various ways of misbehaving extra fun. You may even pull off a trick that’s not on your to-do list by chance! As someone who identifies as lawful good, I did find some mischiefs rather mean-spirited and obnoxious. Nonetheless, I must admit that it was amusing and cathartic to play a character that is deliciously and unassumingly chaotic evil.

The final task was simply surprising, for it explained the goose’s motivation for embarking on its quest. It’s exciting and nail-biting, and it gave me a great sense of accomplishment when I completed it. Although I still had a few items on my “to-do (as well)” list to cross off by the end of the game, I wished there would be an extra area or two in the village for me to explore.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791351437

However, as a keyboard and mouse gamer, I found the default keys configuration uncomfortable. Mouse controls weren’t that great as well. Once I’ve remapped the keys so that I control the goose’s movement with WASD, and reassigned keys for zooming in/out, using the beak, and spreading wings to the arrow keys, the controls felt more natural. Or perhaps I could’ve just used my gaming controller. Oh, well.

I didn’t bother with the game’s time trials, but I took me about 7 hours to complete all shenanigans. It’s a good length for a game with such a simple, entertaining premise. As for the soundtrack -- the thing that got me interested in the game in the first place -- I love how Debussy’s whimsical and lyrical melodies complemented the in-game events so well.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791351069

So, don’t be a fool like I was and think little of [I]Untitled Goose Game[/I]. It’s a game that convinced me to embrace my inner chaotic evil side, taught me the malice that geese are capable of, and showed me that a goose has just as much star appeal as dogs, cats, ducks, rabbits and racoons. [I]Untitled Goose Game[/I] has since become one of my favourite games, and it just may be one of the most entertaining one you’ll play as well.

[h1]The Game in Short[/h1]

You're a goose(or two geese if playing co-op) that run around and attempt to complete tasks with the primary goal of annoying the townspeople.  You are able to move about rather freely and interact with a variety of objects, many of which aren't necessary for you to complete your tasks, they're just there for fun.  It's innocent mischief, without violence or hurting people, nor do the people hurt you.  It's a nice semi-casual game that you can just explore and tinker with to see the townspeople's reactions.  The game has a pretty laid back feeling and has a calm, soothing piano soundtrack.

[h1]How long is it?[/h1]

You will spend a few hours completing this game.  Maybe 5 hours?  You could technically beat the game in under an hour but that would be a speed run if you already know how to complete the tasks.

[h1]How hard is it?[/h1]

The game isn't too hard.  My 4 year old could handle the controls.  Granted, she needed my help figuring out the tasks, but she could perform them with instruction from me.

The achievements are a nice balance between obtainable and challenging.  Don't worry about the mystery achievements until after you've completed the game.  Once you complete the game, the mystery achievements are unveiled and it's more obvious what you need to do for them.  In the end I was able to get all achievements without any outside help or internet searches.

[h1]Good for kids?[/h1]

It's good as a "first game" for a 3 to 4 year old.  My daughter loves the game.  Although it can be a test of patience if youre playing together with a very young child.  All my daughter wants to do is run around and manipulate random objects, which is fine and many times I let her take the lead in just doing random things.  However, keep in mind both geese must stay in relatively close proximity to each other so if you both want to go and do two different things the game becomes a stalemate.  If you want to complete the game make sure your kid is old enough to have any interest in completing the tasks with you, hah!  I had to play some of parts of the game solo when my daughter wasn't around so that I could get the tasks done, opening up other areas for us to explore.

[h1]Replayability?[/h1]

There's a small amount of replayability for this one.  For me, once I got all the achievements I was done.  You've definitely seen everything the game can do at that point.  However, my daughter seemed to enjoy just running around and playing with the various objects, dumping them in the lake or making the townspeople chase her.  That's where a lot of the additional hours I put into the game came from.

[h1]Bugs or crashes?[/h1]

I didn't encounter any bugs when I played it.

[h1]Do I recommend it?[/h1]

It was fun for both me and my daughter.  It's not too long but well worth the $10 I paid for it.

Untitled Goose Game is a pandemic classic. The game was initially teased for the Nintendo Switch, but I held out for the PC release. Design wise, the graphics are charming and cute, with faceless characters that are expressive and visually interesting. I think that the designers nailed the rural, idyllic small town feel of the game. The sound effects are well designed and the music is similarly cute and charming to complement the graphics. Performance was great and likely will be for all but those playing on a Raspberry Pi. 

The puzzles are not overly challenging yet difficult enough to keep you engaged in the game. I played Untitled Goose Game over three 1 hour sessions with my younger sibling and we had a total blast figuring out the puzzles to complete the tasks. Each "scene" in the game is different enough to be interesting on its own. The movement of the goose is simple to manage and allows for perfect heists and acts of slight-of-hand. The game feels like you are playing through an episode of British children's television, and that is not a complaint. Certainly a fun game for anyone, I would recommend playing with a buddy via couch co-op.

[h1] What is this game even about?[/h1] 
Essentially you play as a goose that can pick up smaller objects and drag bigger ones, which is significantly slower.  More than that you can [i]honk[/i] (which is probably the funniest and most addicting part of this game), duck, flap your wings angrily and walk or swim.
Doesn’t necessarily sound like much, but what makes this all the tools you need is an interactive world, in which many things react to what you do. For example, stealing an object of a townsperson and being seen by its owner makes it most likely run after you.

[h1] So what do you want to do with all of this?[/h1] 
It is basically an interactive live-reacting puzzle game. 
You get a handful of objectives on what to do, of which you need to fulfill at least some to go on.
How you achieve your goal is mostly up to you and just figuring out what happens if…
This might sound a tiny bit boring, but is fun with the great piano music scoring to what you do, the always annoyed and/or frustrated townsfolk chasing you or cleaning up after you. 
One’s figured out the puzzles are clear on how to achieve and managing to fulfill them is the next challenge. There is smaller hidden stuff like challenges and just plain fun things you can do and after finishing the game you unlock hidden objectives, to assure some replay value. 

[h1]Replayability[/h1] 
[b]Replayability[/b] is maybe a concern, but the possible co-op gameplay meaning you play as two geese, the pure joy of torturing townsfolk as a goose (such a guilty pleasure I never knew I had) make this title worth its money.

[h1]Style[/h1] 
The game has a distinct simplistic but vibrant [b]style[/b], has calm jazz-like piano music, making every sound different than silence really pop in this environment.
A lot of charm has been put in this game and even after hours there is always one more small detail you might find, of which you never knew. 
It is one of my favorite games even though I really am through with it after nearly 10 hours, but I’d love to revisit with a friend sometime again, to see how they manage and handle this puzzling, [i]honking[/i] fun.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1] 
If you want a relaxing, fun game to play, maybe with a friend, this is what you want.

Im a 27 years old male, I have been living alone since i was 19, when i moved away from my parents and I settled down on a little apartment. Since i was a child, I used to play on the park with my neighbors. We enjoyed one particular game, maybe you have heard of it, it was called "Hide And Seek". The game had 2 roles, the seeker, who has to count to 10, without looking at his enviroment, before starting his duty, and the people who hide as good as they can. The seeker must find all the players hiding, so he can win. 

I don't know if this is a common practice, but when a person was found by the seeker, both of them would run as fast as they could to the counting point, if the person who was hiding got there first, he would be safe, and would win against the seeker. 

Many of my friends played the game normally, hiding, and then running towards the tree where the seeker was counting, sometimes winning, sometimes losing, they had lots of fun doing so, but I didn't. For some reason, playing games as a children was always so boring to me, they never "clicked" for me. But there was something, just one little thing, on that one particular game, one feature that fulfilled my profound desires and yearnings, that was the moment when the seeker founds you. Instead of just running towards the counting point, i would pick the most odd, darkest places for the seeker to go, i went under cars and grabbed the leg of the seeker when he was nearby, up in some trees hiding on the leaves i would jump into them, behind corners, inside bushes... My goal was never to win the game, my goal was to scare the seeker, frighten, terrify, shock this person.

The enjoyment i had on those golden days of my life was taken away from me, because the parents of the kids threatened me, they said their kids were scared of playing with me. Once a child, who got scared of me, ran away and fell down, he got a huge wound on his head, which he still has in the form of a scar. The only thing that fulfilled me, that made me feel alive, probably the only moment of my life where i could be myself, was gone.

The years passed, i got through my life normally. I graduated from middle school, highschool and college. I made normal relationships with everyone, never had a problem at all. But something was missing, this desire, this feeling, this painful need to annoy people, to make then scared, see them cry in fear. This eventually lead me to live my life in a profound emptiness, everyday was just, dull, boring, flat, tasteless. 

I thought my life was doomed to be like this forever, condemned to the boredom. But when i saw this game on the steam store, i saw hope, i saw light. It's not the same than scaring people in real life, but this game provides me joy, it's comforting, it's a dildo that gives pleasure, that satisfy the needs of one of the most deep parts of my soul. 

I recommend this game, than rather than giving me entertainament, gave me life once again. Thank you, Untitled Goose Game.

Untitled Goose Game, where you play as a hecking honking goose and unleash terror on the town. But you already knew that because this game is incredibly popular. I’m not even sure why you’re reading reviews at this point. Just buy the game.

[h1]The Game[/h1] 

The game is a charming puzzle game, with a campaign you can beat in just a few hours. It requires patience and timing… as well as some chaos. Some of the tasks require you to question how you might prank small children, bickering neighbors, and the elderly. There were one or two puzzles I had to google the answer to, but otherwise it’s relatively solve-able if you have the patience (and chaos in your heart). 

Once you beat the main game, there are after-campaign tasks to do. I found these even more enjoyable than the main campaign.  For the achievement hunters, there are timed trials of the campaign puzzles after the main campaign, too.
Mechanics

The game works well with a controller. I didn’t bother using mouse and keyboard – it feels like it was built around a controller. And it game lends itself to sitting back, relaxing, and goosin’ around. There are a couple of areas where it’s easy to get stuck on the environment, which can become frustrating when the puzzle requires timing or finesse. It was nothing game breaking, though. 

[h1]Co-Op[/h1] 

Remote play with co-op is buggy. I wasn’t able to get it work, and it would consistently have one player controlling both Geese. I was able to get shared screen co-op working. The game is delightful with a buddy! 

Co-op allows you to run through the entire game as two Geese. It does make some of the puzzles a little less challenging, since your goose buddy can work as a distraction. But you’re not playing co-op to be a puzzle grand master. You’re playing co-op to double to goose fun. 

I love co-op games and can’t find enough good ones. I do wish there were a couple of co-op specific features, areas, or things to do so I could spend more time in this mode. 

[h1]Cost[/h1]

Depending on how Goose-y you are, the game will probably take you anywhere from 2-5 hours to beat the main campaign. If you want to complete the after-campaign tasks, you’ll get another few hours of fresh, goose game play. 
Games have gotten extremely cheap, and for a 2-10 hour game, $20 might sound expensive. I got it on sale, but the unbridled joy I got from this game, I can confidently say it is worth $20. And you get to support a small, independent video game developer. But if you’re hesitant, it does go on sale pretty often.

Nice game, but due to the fact that you can only get ~10 hours for this game (if you go completion route, do single and coop, and play slowly), I wouldn't recommend it at full price. It is certainly not worth 30$, as good as it is. I would wait for a sale to buy. You would expect that having two people playing at once would make it easier to play, right? Except instead of just split-screening, there's a distance barrier - so essentially, you and your pal are running around, trying to complete tasks, but after running about 20 feet you're stopped by an invisible barrier. So you have to keep close- contact with your partner as you play, which makes multiplayer not that enjoyable (for me at the very least). I am a naturally slow video game player most of the time, but the only reason it took 10 hours was because a) I went completionists route and b) I left the game running as I did things for hours on end. One of the tasks needed for the completionists route is 'complete [level name] before the bell rings' so essentially, complete all the tasks in that area in under 6 minutes. However, aftere much difficulty, I succeeded. Which means, for 4 levels, 4x6 is 24. So if you did every level before the bell rang, you could complete the game in under 30 minutes. 

Thinking about it that way, it doesn't seem worth it to pay $30 for a game the same length. I would recommend waiting for a sale, or better yet, buying a better game with your money.

However, you get out of the game exactly what it says on the store page, so if that's right up your alley and you're itching to waste your money on it, be my guest.

It's charming and good-natured fun. Minimalist art-style and color palette that adds to the charm. Generally pretty funny. A dynamic musical score that emphasizes the mischievous tone. And the gameplay is fun and mostly intuitive. It's a satisfying, comical, puzzle/stealth game that you should buy.

In this game you played a goose wreaking havoc on a small village. It is effectively a puzzle game, where you are given a level of items and humans and specific tasks such as "steal the gardener's hat". Controls are deliberately a little difficult but you get used to them quickly and they add just enough of a challenge to make the game engaging.

The game is quaint, charming, cute, and a million other adjectives like that. Everything goes towards building the aesthetic the game is going for. The art style is simple, with an almost picture book quality to it, that works well. The gameplay is also simple and easily understood, but has enough variety and obstacles to keep you engaged. But what really took it over the top for me is the music. As you do things these little piano snippets play that feel like they narrate what you do! A nice flourish to almost every action.

The game is fairly short, your initial play through will only take about 3 to 4 hours, at which point it will give you a few more tasks that take maybe another hour or two to complete (ignore my play time, I left the game running at one point). The game does not overstay its welcome, so its shortness is probably a good thing, but I know I would have enjoyed a bit more goosey hijinks. But the final sequence of the game that leads you through all previous sections on a chase, is such a perfect ribbon on the experience, I can't be mad. 

This is a game that almost anyone can enjoy. It is simple enough for kids and non-gamers, but does everything so well that even gamers can enjoy it. And some of the achievements are hard enough to even provide a challenge should you need that. A+ all around.

[h1] General Review [/h1]
This is a fun, humorous, chilled-out game. I play it when I'm wanting to game without a serious commitment. It's a short game by any means. I'll credit it for having some fun extra tasks to keep playing even after you complete the main game, but it's still a short game. I've got almost 12 hours but I completed it within 3 or 4, I think.
The only frustration is by design, that humans push you away (physically move your character), the frustration comes when they shove you into a corner or a spot that's hard to get around and run away. My diversion trick is [spoiler] steal the source of the issue (like the broom) and hide it OUTSIDE the area. Just be careful the character doesn't chase you too far, with the item in question [i] or [/i] a different item, because they might find the hidden item & take it back (this happened to me recently). [/spoiler]

[h1] Worth Its Price? [/h1]
I wouldn't buy it at full price. I think I bought it 1/2 off, but I still wish I would've gotten an even better sale, for as short as the game is. I've repeated it, but mostly because it's one of the only chill games I have.

[h1] Summary [/h1]
Pros:
[list]
[*] Stylistic visuals
[*] Easy controls
[*] light-hearted and humorous
[/list]

Cons
[list]
[*] short gameplay
[*] micro-frustrations of character interactions

"Honk!"
Doris stuck her head out of the bush they had been sleeping in as the late summer morning sun came over the trees. Not far from where they slept, a boy with glasses was playing with a ball. 

"Wake up, Pontificus, you lazy ganger!" she honked. "There's  a boy having fun. That just won't do!"
"Sir Pontificus is awake, m'lady" he honked. 

For the strapping ganger he was, Pont was mostly a complete loon. They had been mates since she could lay eggs and never did he loose the dapper persona he had when she first met him on the lake. Some part of her was never sure how much of it was real. It did not matter. He was fun... and clever... and mischievous. 

"For love and seed and honor!"
Her reverie was broken as he suddenly sped out of the bush, seemingly instantly reaching top speed, wings flapping wildly while honking the Ride Of The Valkyries.  
"Nya-nya nyanyanya nya-nya nyanya nya nyaaaaaa!" 

"Hey wait for me!" She honked and sped after him. 
The boy had already started turning to see where the racket was coming from and Doris could see the boy's expression turning from confusion to shock. Shock to terror.  He turned to run. Stumbled. Tripped and landed roughly on the tarmac as Pontificus slammed into him, pecking at his legs. 
Doris had other ideas. With the boy now on the ground she went for his face. After a few pecks, the boy had already curled into the fetal position. His glasses had come loose and just then an idea came to her. 
"Pont! Come" she honked, grabbed the glasses in her beak and bolted around the corner. 
Pont was not far behind when she reached the well. 
"Sir Pontificus found that exhilirating!" he said as he sidled up to her. She already had the glasses held over the lip of the well. 
They always did this together. True love. Forever. 

The glasses dropped with a splosh deep into the water below. 
"Sir Pontificus suggests we get breakfast." he honked while still staring down at the rapidly sinking glasses. 
"Yes Pont. Let's go eat."

The game is woefully short (I achieved 100% within 5 hours), but honestly, it's so chock-full of heart, I didn't mind a bit. It says what it wants to say, and doesn't overstay its welcome. Forget GTA... turns out the real menace to society, is a goose on a mission!

This is a great game to kill an afternoon, it is short and one of the most "casual" games out there. Puzzles are generally easy enough to solve and  the art style is basic but pretty. I enjoyed the audio too, from the goose honks to the piano music that suits the goose's a*hole personality.Another obvious positive for this game is the low-entry barrier in terms of system requirements.

There is re-playability here for sure, as there is no chance you would get all of the extra tasks without using a guide and of course there is the speedrun achievements.

I only have two real negatives, firstly I have a dual monitor setup. I played this game on "fullscreen", but often it would detect that I dragged the cursor off the screen, which meant it I clicked it would minismise the game, which was a bit of a headache.

Also as the game is so short I would expect the price to be a little lower. I got it on sale for a little over €8, but considering there is only 2-3 hours of gameplay (maybe more if you wanted to do the speedrun achievements) I wouldn't recommend paying any more than that.
